title: Analysis and Detection of Stagnation in Floating-Point Summation
summary: Stagnation in the summation of floating-point numbers occurs when the running sum, or the accumulator, does not change its value despite addends being greater than zero. Here we define different types of stagnation - commonly referred to as swamping or absorption, where one operand in an addition is nearly or completely rounded off---in floating-point summation, and propose algorithms for detecting it in numerical code that uses floating-point arithmetic. Whilst cancellation in floating-point arithmetic has been studied, for example by Lam et al. in `Dynamic floating point cancellation detection', stagnation has not been exploited as a property for detecting and reporting accuracy loss in floating-point operations. We have built prototype dynamic stagnation detection tools in two languages, MATLAB and Julia, and applied them to applications ranging from basic summation of a vector, to matrix multiplication, to a fluid flow simulation model. With this tool, users are able to identify areas of their floating-point code where stagnation occurs - in those areas of the code one may need to switch to a higher precision number format, apply stochastic rounding, or use different summation algorithms such as compensated summation. To the best of our knowledge we provide a first rigorous definition of stagnation in floating-point summation.

AI.tldr: This paper rigorously defines stagnation (swamping/absorption) in floating-point summation and presents prototype dynamic detection tools in MATLAB and Julia to identify accuracy loss in numerical code.
AI.motivation: While floating-point cancellation has been studied (e.g., by Lam et al.), stagnation has not been exploited as a property for detecting and reporting accuracy loss in floating-point operations. There is no rigorous definition of stagnation in floating-point summation.
AI.method: The authors define different types of stagnation—where one operand in an addition is nearly or completely rounded off—and propose algorithms for detecting it in numerical code using floating-point arithmetic. They build prototype dynamic stagnation detection tools in two languages, MATLAB and Julia.
AI.result: The tools were applied to applications ranging from basic vector summation, to matrix multiplication, to a fluid flow simulation model. Users can identify areas of their floating-point code where stagnation occurs.
AI.conclusion: Stagnation detection helps pinpoint code regions where one may need to switch to higher precision, apply stochastic rounding, or use alternative summation algorithms such as compensated summation. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this is the first rigorous definition of stagnation in floating-point summation.

title: Multilevel Picard approximations for McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations with jumps
summary: We introduce multilevel Picard (MLP) approximations of McKean-Vlasov stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with jumps of finite or infinite activity. Under Lipschitz and integrability assumptions on the coefficients, we show that the MLP algorithm does not suffer from the curse of dimensionality when approximating the solution of the McKean-Vlasov SDE. The latter means that its computational cost grows at most polynomially in both the state-space dimension of the SDE and the reciprocal of the prescribed error tolerance. In two numerical experiments, we demonstrate the practical applicability of the MLP algorithm for two different McKean-Vlasov SDEs in dimensions up to 200.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces multilevel Picard (MLP) approximations for McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps, proving they avoid the curse of dimensionality and are computationally efficient in high dimensions.
AI.motivation: McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps are important but hard to solve numerically, especially in high dimensions, where standard methods suffer from the curse of dimensionality.
AI.method: The authors develop multilevel Picard (MLP) approximations for McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps of finite or infinite activity, under Lipschitz and integrability assumptions on the coefficients.
AI.result: The MLP algorithm's computational cost grows at most polynomially in both the state-space dimension and the reciprocal of the error tolerance, and numerical experiments demonstrate applicability in dimensions up to 200.
AI.conclusion: MLP approximations provide an efficient, curse-of-dimensionality-free method for solving high-dimensional McKean-Vlasov SDEs with jumps.

title: A Neural-Network Approach for the Stability of Loosely-Coupled FSI Simulations in Hemodynamics
summary: The development of accurate and efficient computational methods for fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems remains an active research area due to its broad engineering and biomedical applications. Partitioned loosely coupled (LC) schemes are attractive for large-scale simulations because of their modularity and low computational cost. However, their applicability is limited by stability issues in high added-mass regimes, where fluid and structure densities are comparable, as in hemodynamics. In our recent work, we proposed an LC algorithm based on Dirichlet-Neumann interface coupling, the LC-DN-α scheme, which improves the stability of the coupling through a stabilization parameter α. Although theoretical stability has been demonstrated under suitable constraints on α, its optimal value depends on the physical and numerical characteristics of the FSI problem and is difficult to determine in practice. In this work, we propose a data-driven strategy to automatically estimate the optimal value of α. We develop a feed-forward neural network to predict α from the descriptors of the FSI problem. The model is trained on a dataset of baseline FSI problems in large added-mass regimes and evaluated on more realistic configurations to assess robustness and generalization. Numerical results show that the proposed model generalizes across the considered FSI scenarios and provides robust estimates of α under moderate variations in the problem setup, including changes in geometry and loading conditions, that do not completely alter the interaction mechanics represented in the training set. The methodology is intentionally developed and validated on simplified FSI problems, providing a proof of concept for data-driven strategies to improve the efficiency of partitioned FSI simulations and supporting their extension to more complex and realistic scenarios.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a data-driven strategy using a feed-forward neural network to automatically estimate the optimal stabilization parameter α in an LC-DN-α partitioned FSI coupling scheme, improving stability in high added-mass regimes without manual tuning.
AI.motivation: Partitioned loosely coupled (LC) schemes for FSI are attractive for large-scale simulations due to modularity and low cost, but suffer stability issues in high added-mass regimes (e.g., hemodynamics). The LC-DN-α scheme improves stability via a parameter α, but its optimal value depends on problem-specific physical/numerical characteristics and is hard to determine in practice.
AI.method: A feed-forward neural network predicts α from descriptors of the FSI problem. It is trained on a dataset of baseline FSI problems in large added-mass regimes and evaluated on more realistic configurations to assess robustness and generalization.
AI.result: The model generalizes across the considered FSI scenarios, providing robust α estimates under moderate variations in problem setup (including geometry and loading conditions) that do not completely alter the interaction mechanics represented in the training set.
AI.conclusion: The methodology is intentionally developed and validated on simplified FSI problems, serving as a proof of concept for data-driven strategies to improve partitioned FSI simulation efficiency and supporting extension to more complex, realistic scenarios.

title: Numerical Neural Operator: Connection Between Numerical Analysis and the Operator Learning and Building Discretized Neural Operators from Finite Element Methods
summary: Operator learning aims to learn mappings between function spaces and has been widely used for PDE-related problems. This raises two fundamental questions. First, is there a connection between standard numerical methods and neural operators, given that both are designed to approximate PDE solution operators? Second, when a neural operator is trained on numerically generated data, does it approximate the underlying infinite dimension operator, the training data themselves, or the discretized numerical scheme used to generate them? A key hypothesis in the paper is that the trained neural operator may mimic the discretized numerical schemes that generate the training data. The hypothesis has been partially and preliminary verified by the linear approximation principle proposed in Chen Chen 1995 paper and the following scaling law papers. However, neural operator approximation from the perspective of numerical discretization remains unexplored. In this work, we consider a class of PDEs and derive neural operator architectures from the numerical schemes. Firstly, the numerical basis functions, such as finite element basis functions, can be approximated or directly constructed by learnable neural networks. Then the finite difference schemes for temporal discretization can be unrolled into iterative neural architectures that generate the coefficients of the basis of the resulting neural operator. By leveraging numerical analysis, we establish convergence error estimates for these numerically derived neural operators. Notably, the network size depends polynomial on the approximation error in $L_2$, improving the nested exponential dependence derived in the general neural operator approximation and aligning with the numerical observations. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate reduced errors and improved parameter efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper connects standard numerical discretization schemes with neural operator architectures, showing that trained neural operators may mimic the discretized schemes generating their training data, and derives architecturally grounded operators with polynomial network-size dependence.
AI.motivation: Two fundamental questions motivate the work: (1) whether there is a connection between standard numerical methods and neural operators, since both approximate PDE solution operators; and (2) whether a neural operator trained on numerically generated data approximates the underlying infinite-dimensional operator, the training data, or the discretized numerical scheme used to generate the data. The hypothesis—partially verified by Chen 1995's linear approximation principle and scaling-law papers—that trained neural operators mimic their generating discretized schemes remains unexplored from a numerical discretization perspective.
AI.method: For a class of PDEs, the authors derive neural operator architectures directly from numerical schemes. Numerical basis functions (e.g., finite element basis functions) are approximated or constructed by learnable neural networks, while finite difference temporal discretization schemes are unrolled into iterative neural architectures that generate the coefficients of the resulting neural operator's basis. Numerical analysis is then used to establish convergence error estimates for these numerically derived neural operators.
AI.result: The derived neural operators achieve convergence error estimates where network size depends polynomially on the L2 approximation error, improving on the nested exponential dependence of general neural operator approximation and aligning with numerical observations. Numerical experiments show reduced errors and improved parameter efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a concrete bridge between numerical discretization schemes and neural operator design, supporting the hypothesis that trained neural operators mimic their generating discretization schemes and yielding more efficient, numerically grounded architectures with favorable approximation guarantees.

title: Reconstruction of Multiscale Plasma Dynamics Across Operating Regimes
summary: Reconstructing spatially resolved plasma dynamics from few sensors is essential for diagnostics, reduced-order modelling and control, yet remains difficult because the sparse measurements incompletely constrain multiscale, regime-dependent degrees of freedom. The Shallow Recurrent Decoder (SHRED) partially addresses spatial sparsity by using measurement histories; however, its fully connected decoder provides no explicit mechanism for resolving spatial structure across scales or explicit parametric dependency. We introduce the Recurrent Multiscale Affine-modulated Inference Network (ReMAIN), which preserves SHRED's recurrent temporal encoding but replaces its decoder with a U-Net whose feature hierarchy is conditioned by the recurrent state through feature-wise linear modulation. The temporal representation supplies both a dense prior and scale-specific modulation throughout the U-Net. A parametric extension jointly embeds the operating condition and sensor history, enabling reconstruction to adapt as the governing dynamics change with operating regime. ReMAIN is first benchmarked against SHRED on six one-dimensional nonlinear PDEs representing diverse dynamics. Across all benchmarks, it reduces reconstruction errors on unseen trajectories and more faithfully resolves sharp transitions, localized extrema and fine-scale variations. The parameter-conditioned model is then demonstrated on a collisionless $E \times B$ plasma subject to perpendicular axial electric and radial magnetic fields, with the electric-field strength serving as the operating parameter. ReMAIN reconstructs the high-dimensional, multiscale plasma state and recovers its regime-dependent spatiotemporal dynamics at electric-field strengths withheld from training. Together, ReMAIN improves sparse-sensor full-state reconstruction and, through parameter conditioning, generalizes across plasma operating regimes.

AI.tldr: ReMAIN replaces SHRED's fully connected decoder with a recurrent-state-conditioned U-Net using FiLM, plus an optional parameter-conditioning branch, improving sparse-sensor full-state reconstruction and enabling generalization across plasma operating regimes.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing spatially resolved plasma dynamics from few sensors is hard because sparse measurements incompletely constrain multiscale, regime-dependent degrees of freedom. SHRED uses measurement histories but its fully connected decoder has no explicit mechanism for multiscale spatial structure or parametric dependency.
AI.method: ReMAIN keeps SHRED's recurrent temporal encoder but replaces the decoder with a U-Net whose feature hierarchy is conditioned by the recurrent state via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), supplying a dense prior and scale-specific modulation. A parametric extension jointly embeds operating condition and sensor history so reconstruction adapts to changing regimes.
AI.result: Benchmarked against SHRED on six 1D nonlinear PDEs, ReMAIN reduces reconstruction errors on unseen trajectories and better resolves sharp transitions, localized extrema, and fine-scale variations. On a collisionless E×B plasma with electric-field strength as operating parameter, it reconstructs the high-dimensional multiscale state and recovers regime-dependent spatiotemporal dynamics at withheld field strengths.
AI.conclusion: ReMAIN improves sparse-sensor full-state reconstruction and, via parameter conditioning, generalizes across plasma operating regimes.

title: Threshold Scattering for the Three-Dimensional Focusing Energy-Critical Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation
summary: Threshold scattering below the ground-state energy and gradient is established for the three-dimensional focusing energy-critical nonlinear Schrödinger equation. A single solution-dependent Gaussian interaction scale, mass-free angular coercivity, and a frequency-gap source estimate control the projected dynamics. These estimates yield quartic spacetime integrability and a zero-mass contradiction, without radial symmetry or an a priori $L^2$ bound.

AI.tldr: Threshold scattering below the ground-state energy is established for the 3D focusing energy-critical NLS using a single solution-dependent Gaussian scale, angular coercivity, and a frequency-gap estimate.
AI.motivation: To prove scattering at threshold for the 3D focusing energy-critical NLS without relying on radial symmetry or an a priori L^2 bound.
AI.method: A solution-dependent Gaussian interaction scale, mass-free angular coercivity, and a frequency-gap source estimate control the projected dynamics.
AI.result: Quartic spacetime integrability and a zero-mass contradiction are obtained.
AI.conclusion: Threshold scattering holds under the established estimates, removing the usual radial and L^2 constraints.

title: Omnisolver: An extensible interface to Ising spin-glass and QUBO solvers: adding a distributed GPU brute-force plugin
summary: This software update extends Omnisolver with \texttt{omnisolver-bruteforce}, a first-class plugin for exact exhaustive search of QUBO and Ising instances on CUDA-enabled GPUs. The update contributes three components: packaging of the single-GPU brute-force kernel of [Computer Physics Communications 260, 107728, 2021] as a first-class Omnisolver plugin with a uniform Python and CLI interface, a Ray-based distributed framework that splits the search into $2^{k}$ fixed-variable subproblems and dispatches them across multiple GPUs and hosts, with a controller that gathers and merges partial results, and numerical stabilization of the fast \texttt{float32} ground-state path through compensated incremental updates, periodic exact energy re-anchoring, and best-buffer refresh. Stabilization activates automatically for $N \geq 40$ leaving the public sampler API is unchanged. On dense random Ising instances we measure exhaustive solve times up to $N=60$ on $8\times$ NVIDIA H100 (96 GB) GPUs, reaching $\approx\!3.15$ days at $N=60$ in close agreement with the empirical $t_{N+1}=2\,t_N$ doubling rule, with the distributed sampler reaching the full $\approx\!8\times$ speedup over a single H100 from $N\!\gtrsim\!44$ onwards. The plugin thereby serves as a practical ground-truth oracle for state-of-the-art classical heuristics such as the Simulated Bifurcation Machine.

AI.tldr: The paper presents omnisolver-bruteforce, an Omnisolver plugin that enables exact exhaustive search of QUBO/Ising instances on CUDA GPUs, extended to a Ray-based multi-GPU/multi-host distributed framework with numerical stabilization for the fast float32 path.
AI.motivation: Exact ground-truth solutions are needed to benchmark state-of-the-art classical heuristics (e.g., SBM), but exhaustive search at large N is computationally prohibitive on single devices and is numerically fragile in fast float32 arithmetic.
AI.method: The update has three parts: (1) packaging a single-GPU brute-force kernel as a first-class Omnisolver plugin with uniform Python/CLI interface; (2) a Ray-based distributed framework splitting the search into 2^k fixed-variable subproblems dispatched across GPUs/hosts with a controller merging results; (3) numerical stabilization of the float32 path via compensated incremental updates, exact energy re-anchoring, and best-buffer refresh, auto-activated for N≥40 with unchanged API.
AI.result: On dense random Ising instances, exhaustive solve times reach up to N=60 on 8× NVIDIA H100 (96 GB) GPUs, about 3.15 days at N=60, matching the t_{N+1}=2t_N doubling rule. The distributed sampler achieves ~8× speedup over a single H100 from N≳44.
AI.conclusion: The plugin provides a practical ground-truth oracle for benchmarking state-of-the-art classical heuristics such as the Simulated Bifurcation Machine.

title: A unified framework for original energy dissipation of equilibrium-preserving exponential Runge--Kutta methods for $L^2$ gradient flows
summary: This paper develops a unified framework for establishing original energy dissipation of equilibrium-preserving exponential time differencing Runge--Kutta (ETDRK) methods for $L^2$ gradient flows. The analysis is based on an auxiliary continuous evolution representation of a general ETDRK method, which allows the energy variation to be controlled without imposing positive-definiteness conditions on the Butcher coefficients or introducing stabilization terms. For a broad class of equilibrium-preserving ETDRK schemes, we derive an explicitly computable time-step restriction. Explicit restrictions are obtained for representative schemes of orders two through five, and the framework also applies to arbitrarily high-order interpolation-based ETDRK methods. For the latter class, the resulting admissible step sizes are substantially larger than those obtained from the previous interpolation-specific analysis. Numerical experiments for the Allen--Cahn equation confirm the theoretical dissipation restrictions.

AI.tldr: A unified framework proves original energy dissipation for equilibrium-preserving ETDRK methods on L² gradient flows, yielding explicit time-step restrictions for orders 2–5 and high-order schemes.
AI.motivation: Previous analyses required positive-definiteness of Butcher coefficients or added stabilization terms, which is restrictive and may not reflect the original scheme's behavior.
AI.method: Introduces an auxiliary continuous evolution representation of general ETDRK methods to control energy variation without positive-definiteness or stabilization assumptions.
AI.result: Derives explicitly computable time-step restrictions for a broad class of equilibrium-preserving ETDRK schemes, with explicit results for orders 2–5 and larger admissible step sizes for interpolation-based high-order methods than prior work. Allen–Cahn experiments confirm the theory.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a general and less restrictive tool for establishing energy dissipation of ETDRK methods, improving admissible step sizes and validated numerically.

title: Beam filamentation instability drives deuterium-tritium fusion with polarized neutron emission
summary: Filamentation instabilities are generally regarded as detrimental to fast-electron transport in fusion plasmas because they increase beam divergence and redistribute deposited energy. Here, we use two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations coupled to a spin-dependent deuterium-tritium fusion module to investigate whether filamentation can instead transfer energy from counterstreaming electrons to prepolarized fusion ions. The simulations show that magnetic filaments, together with longitudinal inductive and transverse charge-separation electric fields, accelerate initially stationary deuterons and tritons to energies at which fusion reactions occur. Over the parameter range examined, the calculated neutron yield increases with the saturated magnetic-field energy. The model further predicts anisotropic, spin-resolved neutron emission. The direction of maximum neutron polarization is approximately perpendicular to the dominant deuterium-tritium collision direction and evolves with the angular distribution of the reacting ions. These results suggest that beam filamentation can couple relativistic-electron energy to fusion ions and that polarized neutron emission may provide a reaction-weighted signature of the underlying plasma dynamics.

AI.tldr: Filamentation instabilities, usually considered harmful to fast-electron transport, are shown via 2D PIC simulations to instead transfer energy from counterstreaming electrons to prepolarized DT ions, driving fusion and producing anisotropic spin-resolved neutron emission.
AI.motivation: Filamentation is conventionally seen as detrimental to fast-electron transport in fusion plasmas because it increases beam divergence and redistributes deposited energy. The authors ask whether it could instead be exploited to transfer energy to prepolarized fusion ions.
AI.method: Two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations coupled to a spin-dependent deuterium-tritium fusion module.
AI.result: Magnetic filaments plus longitudinal inductive and transverse charge-separation electric fields accelerate initially stationary deuterons and tritons to fusion-relevant energies. Neutron yield increases with saturated magnetic-field energy over the studied parameter range. The model predicts anisotropic, spin-resolved neutron emission, with maximum polarization roughly perpendicular to the dominant DT collision direction, evolving with the reacting-ion angular distribution.
AI.conclusion: Beam filamentation can couple relativistic-electron energy to fusion ions, and polarized neutron emission may serve as a reaction-weighted signature of the underlying plasma dynamics.

title: The singular set in the thin Stefan problem
summary:
We study the singular set of the free boundary for solutions of the thin Stefan problem in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\times \mathbb{R}$, which models the melting of a thin sheet of ice over water. After a suitable transformation, we reduce to studying the parabolic Signorini (thin obstacle) problem with a time-monotonicity condition. First, we prove that the free boundary is locally the graph of a differentiable melting function $t=τ(x)$ defined on the $n$-dimensional thin space, and that the singular set coincides with the critical set of $τ$. Next, we show that the singular set has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most $n$. We then establish generic regularity up to dimension $n+1=4$, proving that the free boundary is regular for almost every time. Finally, under smoothness assumptions on the obstacle, we show that the singular set is contained in a $C^\infty$-hypersurface outside a set of parabolic dimension at most $n-1$.
  Our analysis combines ideas developed for the classical Stefan problem with several new ingredients specific to the thin setting, including frequency formulas for second blow-ups, epiperimetric inequalities, higher order expansions, and a fine stratification of the singular set.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the singular set of the free boundary in the thin Stefan problem in R^{n+1}×R, reducing it to a time-monotone parabolic Signorini problem and proving dimension, generic regularity, and stratification results.
AI.motivation: The thin Stefan problem models melting of a thin ice sheet over water, and understanding the structure and size of its free-boundary singular set is a fundamental regularity question. Classical Stefan techniques do not directly suffice in this thin setting, motivating new tools.
AI.method: Via a suitable transformation, the problem is reduced to the parabolic Signorini (thin obstacle) problem with a time-monotonicity condition. The analysis combines frequency formulas for second blow-ups, epiperimetric inequalities, higher-order expansions, and a fine stratification of the singular set.
AI.result: The free boundary is locally a graph of a differentiable melting function t=τ(x), with the singular set equal to the critical set of τ. The singular set has parabolic Hausdorff dimension at most n, and generic regularity holds up to dimension n+1=4 (free boundary regular for almost every time). Under obstacle smoothness, the singular set lies in a C^∞-hypersurface outside a set of parabolic dimension at most n−1.
AI.conclusion: The thin Stefan free boundary is largely regular: its singular set is low-dimensional and, generically, the boundary is regular almost everywhere in time, with strong stratification under smoothness assumptions on the obstacle.

title: Fast Angular Sweep Monostatic Radar Cross Section Computation via Model Order Reduction
summary:
The radar cross section (RCS) is a fundamental parameter in radar engineering, as it determines the detectability of a given target by a radar system. Increasing interest in very low observability (VLO) targets has arisen recently. As a result, especial effort is put in developing numerical tools to accurately predict the electromagnetic scattering from perfect electric conductor objects. Integral equation methods are commonly used in this task. However, full-wave computation of the monostatic RCS at a single angle can be rather time-consuming, nevermind computing the RCS in a specific angular interval with a fine sampling. In fact, this is what is needed in industrial applications.
  A reduced-order model for fast full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation is proposed to easily achieve fine details in the desired angular domain. An open source integral equation solver, taken into account as a black box, is used to get the electromagnetic scattering in non-penetrable objects at some specific incident angles. Several radar targets will show the possibilities and capabilities of these model order reduction approaches.

AI.tldr: A reduced-order model is proposed to rapidly evaluate full-wave monostatic RCS over a fine angular interval, using an open-source integral equation solver as a black box.
AI.motivation: RCS determines target detectability, and interest in very low observability (VLO) targets has grown. Accurate full-wave prediction of scattering from perfect electric conductor objects is needed, but computing monostatic RCS at a single angle is already costly—let alone computing it over an angular interval with fine sampling, as industrial applications require.
AI.method: A reduced-order model for fast full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation is proposed to capture fine angular detail. An open-source integral equation solver is treated as a black box to obtain the electromagnetic scattering of non-penetrable objects at a few specific incident angles. Several radar targets are used to demonstrate the capabilities of these model order reduction approaches.
AI.result: The proposed model order reduction approaches are demonstrated on several radar targets, showing their possibilities and capabilities for fast full-wave monostatic RCS evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Model order reduction enables efficient, fine-resolution monostatic RCS computation over a desired angular domain using a black-box integral equation solver, addressing the computational bottleneck of industrial RCS analysis.

title: Quantitative finite-time approximation of scattering fields for Alfvén waves in ideal MHD
summary: In this paper, we establish a quantitative finite-time approximation of scattering fields for nonlinear Alfvén waves in three-dimensional ideal incompressible magnetohydrodynamics near a strong constant magnetic background. Using the global weighted estimates, we prove that truncating the scattering profiles at time $T$ introduces an error in both the $L^\infty$ norm and the $H^{N_*+1}$ norm of order $$ O\bigl(\varepsilon^2(R+T)^{-δ}\bigr), $$ where $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ measures the size of the initial perturbation, $R\ge100$ is the scale parameter in the weighted energy, $δ\in(0,2/3)$ is the exponent related to weights, and $N_*+1$ is the Sobolev regularity order assumed for the initial data. The pointwise estimate follows from the decay of the nonlocal pressure along nonlinear characteristics, while the Sobolev estimate combines higher-order weighted pressure bounds with estimates for derivatives of the characteristic flows. Numerical experiments measure pointwise and Sobolev pressure-integral tails to verify the quadratic dependence of the initial perturbation amplitude.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a quantitative finite-time approximation of scattering fields for nonlinear Alfvén waves in 3D ideal incompressible MHD near a strong constant magnetic background, with error O(ε²(R+T)^(-δ)).
AI.motivation: To quantitatively approximate scattering fields for nonlinear Alfvén waves in 3D ideal incompressible MHD near a strong constant magnetic background, controlling truncation error.
AI.method: Uses global weighted estimates. Pointwise estimate derived from decay of nonlocal pressure along nonlinear characteristics; Sobolev estimate combines higher-order weighted pressure bounds with estimates for derivatives of characteristic flows.
AI.result: Truncating scattering profiles at time T yields error O(ε²(R+T)^(-δ)) in both L∞ and H^{N_*+1} norms. Numerical experiments confirm quadratic dependence on initial perturbation amplitude.
AI.conclusion: Quasi-optimal finite-time approximation of scattering fields is established, with numerical verification of the predicted quadratic amplitude dependence.

title: Reaching high fusion gain with grams of spin-polarized fuel
summary: Building on recent ignition-access work of Delgado-Aparicio, Ono, and Menard, we show that even a single-use, gram-scale quantity of spin-polarized fuel (SPF) is useful for increasing fusion power and gain in magnetic confinement fusion machines such as tokamaks and stellarators. While fueling a fusion power plant continuously with SPF requires $\sim$kilograms per day, far beyond present capabilities, a single-use short pulse of SPF allows a fusion plasma to cross into a high-gain regime, and stay there, even after switching back to regular unpolarized fuel. With continuous polarized fueling, polarization also makes high-gain plasmas easier to control: a resonant wave that depolarizes the fuel lowers the reactivity quickly, on a much faster timescale than transport. Grams of polarized fuel can therefore improve plasma performance and open a path to scaling SPF sources and usage, from small first experiments to continuous fueling.

AI.tldr: A single-use gram-scale pulse of spin-polarized fuel can push magnetic confinement fusion plasmas into a high-gain regime and keep them there, even after reverting to regular fuel; continuous polarized fueling also improves control.
AI.motivation: Continuous SPF fueling at plant scale requires kilograms per day, far beyond present capabilities. The authors seek an achievable, near-term use of SPF despite limited source output.
AI.method: Building on ignition-access work by Delgado-Aparicio, Ono, and Menard, they analyze fusion power and gain in tokamaks and stellarators under single-use (gram-scale) SPF pulses, and examine control via resonant depolarizing waves.
AI.result: A single gram-scale SPF pulse lets the plasma cross into a high-gain regime and remain there after switching back to unpolarized fuel. With continuous polarized fueling, a resonant depolarizing wave lowers reactivity quickly, faster than transport timescales.
AI.conclusion: Grams of polarized fuel can improve plasma performance and provide a pathway to scaling SPF sources and usage from small first experiments toward continuous fueling.

title: Elliptic problems involving a diffusion operator of vectorial $p\&q$-Laplacian type
summary: We study a broad class of anisotropic Dirichlet problems driven by the nonhomogeneous operator \[ \mathcal L_Au=-\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_i\!\left( a_i(|\partial_i u|^{p_i})|\partial_i u|^{p_i-2} \partial_i u\right), \] where the functions $a_i$ satisfy structural growth and monotonicity conditions of $(p_i,q_i)$-type. This framework contains, among other examples, the anisotropic $\vec p$-Laplacian, the orthotropic $p\&q$-Laplacian, and anisotropic operators combining several directional growth regimes. We first establish a comparison principle adapted to this lack of homogeneity. For power nonlinearities, including the singular range, we then obtain nonexistence, existence, singular uniqueness, comparison alternatives, and multiplicity results according to the position of the reaction exponent relative to the anisotropic growth and critical exponents. In particular, an intermediate power regime exhibits nonexistence for small positive parameters and two distinct nontrivial solutions for large parameters without additional restrictions on the smallest effective exponent. At partial resonance, $r=p_1<p_N$, we identify an exact positive parameter threshold: there are no nontrivial solutions at or below it, whereas each parameter above it admits infinitely many pairs of solutions converging strongly to zero. We also treat concave--convex reactions with subcritical or critical growth and prove the existence of nontrivial nonnegative weak solutions in the corresponding parameter ranges. The arguments combine a convexity method of Díaz--Saa type, anisotropic Sobolev embeddings, direct minimization, Ekeland's variational principle, mountain-pass techniques, and concentration--compactness.

AI.tldr: The paper studies anisotropic Dirichlet problems driven by a nonhomogeneous operator with (p_i,q_i)-type structural conditions, establishing comparison principles, existence/nonexistence/multiplicity and resonance results for power and concave-convex reactions.
AI.motivation: The operator lacks homogeneity and combines several directional growth regimes, so standard comparison principles and critical-exponent theory do not directly apply. The aim is to develop a unified framework covering anisotropic p-Laplacian, orthotropic p&q-Laplacian, and mixed directional growth operators.
AI.method: A convexity method of Díaz–Saa type, anisotropic Sobolev embeddings, direct minimization, Ekeland's variational principle, mountain-pass techniques, and concentration–compactness arguments.
AI.result: A comparison principle is established for the nonhomogeneous setting. For power reactions, results include nonexistence, existence, singular uniqueness, comparison alternatives and multiplicity, depending on the reaction exponent versus anisotropic growth/critical exponents. An intermediate regime gives nonexistence for small parameters and two nontrivial solutions for large parameters. At partial resonance r=p_1<p_N, an exact threshold yields no nontrivial solutions at or below it and infinitely many vanishing solution pairs above it. Concave–convex reactions with subcritical or critical growth admit nontrivial nonnegative weak solutions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed anisotropic framework and techniques successfully characterize solvability thresholds and multiplicity across several growth regimes without extra restrictions on the smallest effective exponent.

title: Ghost tasking for parametrized Gaussian Processes solving linear differential equations
summary: Physics-informed machine learning has gained significant attention in recent years. In regimes of limited data, parametrized Gaussian processes have become popular. Existing approaches, however, often face limitations, such as requiring parametrizable (also called controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks. In this work, we introduce a systematic procedure we call "ghost tasking", using auxiliary tasks to circumvent these limitations. We prove that such ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes while keeping the number of required tasks (i.e. output dimensions) and latent functions low. We find that ghost tasking performs especially well in an inverse problem setting, even with very few available data. We show the usage and power of ghost tasking in three experiments, providing systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. We provide necessary syntax and explications for two computer algebra programs that compute parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients. Our theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces "ghost tasking," a systematic procedure using auxiliary tasks to make any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling parametrized Gaussian Processes with few tasks and latent functions.
AI.motivation: Existing physics-informed machine learning approaches for limited-data regimes, such as parametrized Gaussian processes, face limitations: they require parametrizable (controllable) systems or a large number of output tasks.
AI.method: The authors introduce "ghost tasking," using auxiliary (ghost) tasks. They prove ghost tasks can render any non-parametrizable system effectively parametrizable, enabling algorithmic construction of parametrized Gaussian Processes with low numbers of tasks and latent functions. They also provide syntax for two computer algebra programs computing parametrizations for systems with polynomial or rational coefficients.
AI.result: Ghost tasking performs especially well in inverse problem settings, even with very few data. It is demonstrated in three experiments with systematic comparisons to the only other currently available method applicable to all experiments. Theoretical results extend to systems with meromorphic functions.
AI.conclusion: Ghost tasking overcomes key limitations of existing parametrized Gaussian process approaches, enabling effective parametrization of arbitrary systems and strong performance in data-scarce inverse problems.

title: CutIGA with Least Squares Stabilized Nitsche Boundary Conditions: The Biharmonic Problem
summary: We propose a symmetric Nitsche method for the biharmonic Dirichlet problem on a smooth domain whose boundary may cut arbitrarily through the computational mesh. Bulk least-squares stabilization in a boundary strip and tangential boundary penalties control the consistency terms through an explicit lifting of the two Dirichlet traces. This gives coercivity on $H^4(Ω)$ without inverse inequalities and permits a fixed penalty independent of the cut configuration for sufficiently thin strips. Under suitable regularity assumptions, splines of degree $p\geq4$ give energy and $L^2$ error bounds of orders $h^{p-1}$ and $h^{p+1}$. We also analyze a face-stabilized extension to $C^1$ splines of degree $p=2$ and $C^2$ splines of degree $p=3$. Exact-ellipse experiments examine convergence, cut stability, and parameter sensitivity.

AI.tldr: A symmetric Nitsche method is proposed for the biharmonic Dirichlet problem on smooth domains with boundaries cutting arbitrarily through the mesh, using bulk least-squares stabilization and tangential boundary penalties to achieve coercivity on H^4(Ω) without inverse inequalities and a cut-independent penalty.
AI.motivation: The biharmonic Dirichlet problem on domains whose boundary may cut arbitrarily through the computational mesh is challenging: standard Nitsche-type consistency terms require control that usually relies on inverse inequalities or cut-dependent penalties. The authors aim for a method that remains coercive and stable regardless of how the boundary intersects the mesh.
AI.method: A symmetric Nitsche method with bulk least-squares stabilization in a boundary strip plus tangential boundary penalties. Consistency terms are controlled via an explicit lifting of the two Dirichlet traces, giving coercivity on H^4(Ω) without inverse inequalities and allowing a fixed penalty independent of the cut configuration for sufficiently thin strips. Splines of degree p>=4 are analyzed, and a face-stabilized extension to C^1 (p=2) and C^2 (p=3) splines is also studied.
AI.result: Under suitable regularity assumptions, splines of degree p>=4 yield energy and L^2 error bounds of orders h^{p-1} and h^{p+1}, respectively. Exact-ellipse experiments verify convergence, cut stability, and parameter sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The symmetric Nitsche method delivers a cut-stable, coercive discretization of the biharmonic Dirichlet problem with optimal-order spline error estimates and a penalty that is independent of the boundary-mesh cut configuration.

title: The Richtmyer-Meshkov Instability of Thermal, Isotope, and Species Interfaces in a five-moment multi-fluid plasma
comment: Journal of Fluid Mechanics , Volume 951 , 25 November 2022 , A11
summary: The Richtmyer-Meshkov instability (RMI) results from the impulsive acceleration of a density interface where either it or the acceleration is perturbed. Density interfaces may arise due to a change in gas species, isotope, temperature or a combination of these. We computationally investigate the effect of interface type on the plasma RMI, which is relevant for a range of applications, including inertial confinement fusion. We simulate the evolution of single-mode perturbed thermal, species and isotope interfaces in an ideal ion-electron plasma using the multi-fluid plasma (MFP) model. We find that in the MFP model, the evolution of different types of interface differ significantly, in contrast to single-fluid models where they behave similarly if the Atwood number is matched. The thermal and species interfaces produce the most severe response to shock acceleration, experiencing the secondary instabilities and enhanced primary mode growth. The isotope interface evolution is restrained in comparison to the former cases, resembling the response predicted by single-fluid models. The determining factor in the severity of the MFP RMI is the density ratio across the initial interface in the electron fluid, which is unity for an isotope interface. We observe that as the density ratio across the electron interface decreases, so do the magnitudes of the self-generated fields and consequently the severity of the growth amplification. Generally, the evolution of the RMI with different types of interface becomes more similar as the level of coupling between the ion and electron fluids is increased, characterised by reducing the plasma non-dimensional skin depth

AI.tldr: This paper computationally studies how interface type (thermal, species, isotope) affects the plasma Richtmyer-Meshkov instability using a multi-fluid plasma model, showing that electron density ratio across the interface governs the severity, unlike single-fluid predictions.
AI.motivation: Density interfaces in plasmas can arise from changes in gas species, isotope, temperature, or combinations. Single-fluid models treat these interfaces similarly when the Atwood number is matched, but this assumption may fail in plasmas where ion and electron fluids respond differently—relevant to inertial confinement fusion and other applications.
AI.method: Simulate single-mode perturbed thermal, species, and isotope interfaces in an ideal ion-electron plasma using the multi-fluid plasma (MFP) model, tracking the RMI evolution under shock acceleration.
AI.result: Different interface types evolve significantly differently in the MFP model. Thermal and species interfaces show the most severe response, with secondary instabilities and enhanced primary mode growth. The isotope interface is restrained, resembling single-fluid predictions. The key factor is the electron fluid density ratio across the interface—unity for isotope interfaces. Lower electron density ratios reduce self-generated fields and growth amplification. As ion-electron coupling increases (smaller plasma skin depth), the evolution across interface types converges.
AI.conclusion: The electron density ratio across the interface determines the severity of the plasma RMI, explaining why interface types differ in multi-fluid but not single-fluid models. Stronger ion-electron coupling makes the results converge toward single-fluid behavior.

title: A Homogenized Maz'ya--Shaposhnikova formula
summary: We study the asymptotic behaviour of fractional Gagliardo-type energies with a periodic, bounded and bounded away from zero coefficient depending on both variables, in the joint limit of vanishing fractional exponent $s\to0^+$ and vanishing period $\varepsilon\to0^+$. Assuming without loss of generality that $\varepsilon^{-2s}$ converges to some $λ\in[1,+\infty]$, we prove that the energies, rescaled by $s$, $Γ$-converge in the weak topology of $L^2(\mathbb{R}^d)$ to a multiple of the squared $L^2$ norm, whose constant is given by an effective coefficient $a_λ$ defined through a cell problem. The coefficient $a_λ$ results from the competition between the averaging of long-range interactions, which drives the Maz'ya--Shaposhnikova limit, and the nonlocal energy of microscopic oscillations at finite range. It interpolates between the harmonic mean ($λ=1$) and the arithmetic mean ($λ=+\infty$) of a coefficient obtained by averaging interactions ``at infinity''. The proof relies on Riemann--Lebesgue-type lemmas for singular kernels, on a blow-up argument for the lower bound, and on the logarithmic-scaling properties of the energies. The case $1<p<\infty$ is also discussed.

AI.tldr: The paper studies fractional Gagliardo-type energies with a periodic coefficient in the joint limit s→0+ and ε→0+, proving Γ-convergence (after rescaling by s) in the weak L² topology to a multiple of the squared L² norm with constant a_λ given by a cell problem.
AI.motivation: To understand the asymptotic behavior of nonlocal (fractional) energies with oscillating periodic coefficients as both the fractional exponent vanishes and the period shrinks, capturing the competition between long-range averaging and microscopic nonlocal oscillations.
AI.method: Uses Riemann–Lebesgue-type lemmas for singular kernels, a blow-up argument for the lower bound, and logarithmic-scaling properties of the energies; assumes ε^{-2s}→λ and performs Γ-convergence analysis via a cell problem.
AI.result: The s-rescaled energies Γ-converge in weak L² to a multiple of the squared L² norm with effective constant a_λ, which interpolates between the harmonic mean (λ=1) and the arithmetic mean (λ=+∞) of a coefficient obtained by averaging interactions at infinity. The case 1<p<∞ is also discussed.
AI.conclusion: The effective coefficient arises from competition between averaging long-range interactions (Maz'ya–Shaposhnikova limit) and nonlocal energy of microscopic oscillations, yielding an interpolation result; the case 1<p<∞ extends the analysis.

title: NEMORA: Neural Equivariant Multipole Operators for Long-Range Atomistic Learning
summary: Equivariant graph neural networks have emerged as foundational architectures for machine-learned interatomic potentials, approaching quantum-chemical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. These models describe local atomic environments accurately, but finite spatial cutoffs truncate long-range information flow, and stacking message-passing layers can lead to over-smoothing and over-squashing. Existing long-range extensions either prescribe a fixed analytical propagation kernel, restrict long-range communication to scalars or degree-preserving channels, are only approximately equivariant, or incur super-linear computational cost. Combining learnable long-range equivariant transport with multiscale many-body expressivity and efficient scaling for larger systems remains a central challenge. We introduce Neural Equivariant Multipole Operators (NEMORA), a neural equivariant extension of the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) for learning long-range tensorial representations. NEMORA generalizes the FMM's analytical multipole expansion and translation operators to learned equivariant counterparts on an adaptive spatial hierarchy. Its operators couple angular degrees and form many-body interactions across length scales, retaining the FMM's hierarchical organization and analytical radial factors as physical inductive biases while learning data-dependent long-range couplings. NEMORA evaluates in linear time and memory complexity, allowing it to treat larger systems than other long-range methods reaching hundreds of thousands of atoms, and it augments both symmetry-constrained and unconstrained short-range backbones. On non-local benchmarks, it reduces force and energy errors relative to the short-range backbones by over an order of magnitude and up to three orders of magnitude, respectively, which is better than or competitive with existing long-range extensions in accuracy.

AI.tldr: NEMORA is a learned equivariant extension of the Fast Multipole Method that gives equivariant GNN interatomic potentials full long-range tensorial coupling at linear time and memory complexity, cutting force and energy errors by over one to three orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Equivariant GNNs for interatomic potentials are accurate but limited: finite cutoffs truncate long-range information, stacking layers causes over-smoothing and over-squashing. Existing long-range extensions use fixed kernels, restrict to scalars or degree-preserving channels, are only approximately equivariant, or scale super-linearly. Combining learnable long-range equivariant transport, multiscale many-body expressivity, and efficient scaling is an open challenge.
AI.method: NEMORA generalizes the Fast Multipole Method's analytical multipole expansion and translation operators into learned equivariant counterparts on an adaptive spatial hierarchy. Its operators couple angular degrees and form many-body interactions across length scales, retaining FMM's hierarchical organization and analytical radial factors as physical inductive biases while learning data-dependent long-range couplings. It augments both symmetry-constrained and unconstrained short-range backbones.
AI.result: NEMORA runs in linear time and memory, scaling to larger systems than other long-range methods (hundreds of thousands of atoms). On non-local benchmarks it reduces force and energy errors relative to short-range backbones by over one order of magnitude and up to three orders of magnitude, respectively, matching or beating existing long-range extensions.
AI.conclusion: NEMORA offers an accurate, efficient, and scalable long-range equivariant message-passing method for machine-learned interatomic potentials, unifying learnable long-range tensorial transport with multiscale many-body expressivity.

title: A Localized Hybrid Finite Element--Random Feature Method for Elliptic Interface Problems on Unfitted Meshes
summary: We develop a localized hybrid finite element--random feature method (FEM--RFM) for elliptic interface problems on unfitted background meshes. The central idea is to use the random feature method (RFM) only in the narrow band formed by interface-cut cells of a uniform Cartesian background mesh,while retaining standard $Q_p$ finite elements on the remaining uncut cells. Within the band, local RFM representations are used on the two physical sides of the interface. The prescribed jumps in the solution and normal flux are incorporated through residual equations involving the two RFM representations on the physical interface $Γ$, while the finite element method (FEM) and RFM components are coupled across a separate grid-aligned artificial interface $Γ_c$ through trace and variational normal-flux residuals. A Schur reduction eliminates the interior finite element unknowns through sparse solves while retaining their Galerkin equations as equality constraints. The remaining band and interface residuals are minimized in a reduced least-squares problem involving only the coupling nodal values and random-feature coefficients. The method is assessed numerically on a range of two- and three-dimensional interface problems involving high coefficient contrasts, nonsmooth and multiple interfaces, and irregular outer boundaries, together with an application-oriented thermal-homogenization problem for a periodic bicontinuous composite.

AI.tldr: A localized hybrid FEM–RFM method for elliptic interface problems on unfitted meshes, using RFM only in interface-cut bands and FEM elsewhere, coupled via residuals and solved by least squares.
AI.motivation: Elliptic interface problems on unfitted meshes are challenging, especially with high coefficient contrasts and complex/nonsmooth interfaces. A method is needed that handles these robustly while keeping efficiency.
AI.method: Hybrid FEM–RFM: standard Qp FEM on uncut cells of a uniform Cartesian background mesh; local RFM representations on both physical sides of the interface within the narrow cut-cell band. Jumps in solution and normal flux enforced via residual equations on the physical interface Γ; FEM and RFM coupled across a grid-aligned artificial interface Γc via trace and variational normal-flux residuals. Schur reduction eliminates interior FE unknowns (sparse solves), keeping their Galerkin equations as equality constraints. Remaining band/interface residuals minimized in a reduced least-squares problem over coupling nodal values and random-feature coefficients.
AI.result: Numerical assessment on 2D and 3D interface problems with high coefficient contrasts, nonsmooth and multiple interfaces, irregular outer boundaries, and an application-oriented thermal-homogenization problem for a periodic bicontinuous composite.
AI.conclusion: The localized hybrid FEM–RFM provides an effective unfitted-mesh approach for elliptic interface problems, demonstrating versatility across challenging 2D/3D cases and composite homogenization applications.

title: Contributions of the breathing waveform and residual fluctuations to power and higher-order spectra in a Hall-thruster plume
summary: Higher-frequency power in Hall-thruster plume-probe signals can arise from both harmonics of a repeatable breathing waveform and fluctuations about it, complicating spectral interpretation. We decompose 197 paired records from 20 sequentially sampled probe-pair geometries at one operating condition, estimating each phaseconditioned waveform from other records at the same geometry. The residual accounts for 87.1% and 99.7% of measured power in the 0.2-0.5 and 0.5-1 MHz bands, respectively, as medians across geometries. The repeatable waveform, however, reproduces the principal breathing-harmonic bicoherence structure. Residual power remains modulated by breathing phase after waveform removal, exceeding geometry-specific 95thpercentile circular-shift thresholds in both bands at all 20 geometries. Residual bicoherence is substantially weaker than that of the measured signal but exceeds record-specific random-phase thresholds in 195 of 197 records. An exact component expansion further shows that the all-waveform term dominates a specified signed third-order statistic over the fixed 50-80 kHz band near the second breathing harmonic. These results distinguish band-power allocation from harmonic organization within the evaluated frequency ranges. The attribution concerns uncalibrated probe-chain signals and does not identify distinct physical modes or measure energy-transfer rates. The findings motivate assessing repeatable-waveform contributions before interpreting breathing-harmonic bicoherence as evidence of interactions among residual fluctuations.

AI.tldr: The paper decomposes Hall-thruster plume-probe signals into a repeatable breathing waveform and residual fluctuations, showing that the repeatable waveform dominates band power and reproduces principal bicoherence structure, while residual power remains breathing-phase modulated. This cautions against interpreting breathing-harmonic bicoherence as evidence of interactions among residual fluctuations.
AI.motivation: Higher-frequency power in Hall-thruster plume-probe signals can originate from both harmonics of a repeatable breathing waveform and fluctuations about that waveform, which complicates spectral interpretation. Distinguishing band-power allocation from harmonic organization is needed to avoid misinterpreting bicoherence as evidence of interactions among residual fluctuations.
