title: Boundary integral equation based solvers for elastic transmission problems in complex media
summary: We present a boundary integral equation (BIE) framework for two-dimensional time-harmonic elastic transmission problems. Using the Helmholtz decomposition, the elastodynamic displacement fields are expressed in terms of scalar pressure and shear potentials, so that only the four classical Helmholtz boundary integral operators are needed. The key step is a rewriting of the Navier traction operator in the local normal--tangential frame of the interface, in which second-order normal derivatives are eliminated in favour of tangential derivatives and curvature terms. This leads to a one-parameter family of indirect combined field integral equations, depending on a coupling constant $α\ne 0$, which we prove to be uniquely solvable. The principal part of the resulting operator is, however, defective, and the discretized systems are severely ill-conditioned. Using the pseudodifferential calculus of the Helmholtz BIOs, we construct explicit left and right analytical preconditioners and prove that the preconditioned operator is a compact perturbation of the identity. Numerical experiments based on high-order Nyström discretizations confirm that the preconditioner clusters the spectrum: the number of GMRES iterations becomes independent of the discretization and is reduced by one order of magnitude or more, also in the high-frequency regime and for non-convex scatterers.

AI.tldr: A BIE framework for 2D time-harmonic elastic transmission problems using Helmholtz decomposition, with analytical preconditioners that yield discretization-independent GMRES convergence.
AI.motivation: Standard boundary integral formulations for elastic transmission problems suffer from ill-conditioned discretized systems due to a defective principal part, motivating the need for effective preconditioning.
AI.method: Elastodynamic fields are expressed via scalar pressure and shear potentials (Helmholtz decomposition), requiring only the four classical Helmholtz BIOs. The Navier traction operator is rewritten in the local normal-tangential frame, eliminating second-order normal derivatives. This yields a one-parameter family of indirect combined field integral equations, proven uniquely solvable. Using pseudodifferential calculus of Helmholtz BIOs, explicit left/right analytical preconditioners are constructed.
AI.result: The preconditioned operator is proven to be a compact perturbation of the identity. High-order Nyström discretization experiments confirm the preconditioner clusters the spectrum: GMRES iterations become discretization-independent and are reduced by one order of magnitude or more, including in high-frequency regimes and for non-convex scatterers.
AI.conclusion: The proposed BIE framework with analytical preconditioners provides an efficient and robust numerical method for 2D elastic transmission problems, achieving spectrally clustered and discretization-robust iterative solutions.

title: Direct Numerical Comparison of Data Driving Strategies for Solar Flux Emergence in Magnetohydrodynamics: B-driving vs E-driving
summary: Data driving is an important technique for modelling realistic magnetic field and plasma evolution in regions of the solar atmosphere where direct observations are either absent or insufficient. This technique uses observational data to drive the evolution of the simulation, while the modelled solar atmosphere evolves self-consistently. A common approach for data-driven simulations is B-driving, which uses the observed magnetic field at the surface of the Sun as a boundary condition. However, only prescribing B at the boundary does not generally determine its numerical evolution when the update depends on the reconstructed interface states or fluxes. To address this, E-driving provides an alternative approach by instead driving the simulation using the electric field on the boundary, which directly controls the magnetic field update. We systematically quantify the performance of B- and E-driving in a controlled set of numerical experiments. We test both methods in the Athena++ solver using (a) an analytical flux-emergence model (Y. Fan & S. Gibson 2003) and (b) a "ground-truth" reference simulation (S. Toriumi & S. Takasao 2017; S. Toriumi et al. 2020) of active region emergence. For E-driving, the electric field is incorporated into Athena++'s constrained-transport (CT) update, preserving the discrete solenoidal constraint. We assess the reproduction of (i) boundary magnetic flux, (ii) relative magnetic helicity, (iii) total and free magnetic energy, and (iv) magnetic morphology. Across these diagnostics, E-driving gives better overall reproduction of the reference evolution than B-driving. For the configurations considered in an Eulerian CT scheme, E-driving is more accurate than the commonly used ghost-cell B-driving strategies and simpler than constructing an update-consistent B-driving boundary condition.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically compares B-driving and E-driving approaches for data-driven solar magnetic field simulations, finding E-driving reproduces reference evolution more accurately.
AI.motivation: Data-driven simulations of the solar atmosphere require observational data to drive evolution where direct observations are absent. The common B-driving approach only prescribes the surface magnetic field, which does not fully determine its numerical evolution when updates depend on reconstructed interface states or fluxes.
AI.method: The authors test B-driving versus E-driving in Athena++ using (a) an analytical flux-emergence model and (b) a ground-truth reference simulation of active region emergence. For E-driving, the electric field is incorporated into Athena++'s constrained-transport update, preserving the discrete solenoidal constraint.
AI.result: Across diagnostics—boundary magnetic flux, relative magnetic helicity, total and free magnetic energy, and magnetic morphology—E-driving gives better overall reproduction of the reference evolution than B-driving.
AI.conclusion: For Eulerian constrained-transport schemes, E-driving is more accurate than common ghost-cell B-driving strategies and simpler than constructing an update-consistent B-driving boundary condition.

title: From the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation to the Euler-Maxwell equation in the semiclassical limit
summary: We derive the pressureless Euler-Maxwell system as a semiclassical limit from the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation. The method relies on studying a quantum modulated energy accounting for the self-consistent magnetic effects. Crucially, a correction is incorporated in the quantum modulated energy as to enable to close the Grönwall estimate provided a smallness assumption on the initial data is imposed. This is the first result on the semiclassical limit of the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation avoiding any regularization or conditional uniform in $\hbar$ bounds on the wave

AI.tldr: The pressureless Euler-Maxwell system is derived as a semiclassical limit of the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation using a quantum modulated energy method with a magnetic correction term.
AI.motivation: To rigorously connect the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation to the pressureless Euler-Maxwell system, avoiding prior assumptions like regularization or conditional uniform-in-ℏ bounds on the wave function.
AI.method: A quantum modulated energy incorporating self-consistent magnetic effects is studied, with a correction added to close the Grönwall estimate under a smallness assumption on initial data.
AI.result: The semiclassical limit is established, providing the first such derivation without regularization or conditional uniform-in-ℏ wave bounds.
AI.conclusion: The work gives a new, more general rigorous derivation of the pressureless Euler-Maxwell system from quantum dynamics.

title: Femtosecond Three-Dimensional Imaging of Single-Protein with Hard X-ray Laser
summary: The extremely intense pulses of X-ray free-electron lasers (XFELs) have enabled imaging of radiation-sensitive samples, such as macromolecular microcrystals, beyond radiation damage limits. These sources have the potential to deliver biomolecular single-particle imaging, similar to cryo-electron microscopy but without the need for cryo-fixation and with temporal resolution from femtoseconds to milliseconds. While this possibility was recognized before XFELs were built, the biological single-particle imaging work-flow has previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles. Based on decades of improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, here we demonstrate imaging of a single molecular complex, the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses. Two-dimensional classes of diffraction patterns could be reconstructed to 15 Angstrom resolution, and 3D images to approximately 20 Angstrom, while the 3D merged intensity in reciprocal space extended beyond 20 Angstrom. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity caused by gas-phase compaction of the complexes. With increased throughput, this approach could be used to reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules, while improvements in sample delivery may provide ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single-particles in their native-state beyond the limitations of radiation damage.

AI.tldr: This work demonstrates single-particle imaging of a single molecular complex (giant hemoglobin erythrocruorin) using X-ray free-electron laser pulses, achieving 15 Å 2D and ~20 Å 3D resolution, advancing beyond prior large-virus imaging.
AI.motivation: XFELs enable imaging radiation-sensitive samples beyond damage limits and could deliver biomolecular single-particle imaging without cryo-fixation and with femtosecond-to-millisecond temporal resolution. However, this workflow had previously only been demonstrated on large virus particles.
AI.method: Leveraging decades of improvements in X-ray beam focusing, particle delivery, diffraction detection, and advanced analysis, the authors imaged the giant-hemoglobin erythrocruorin (Ery) with X-ray laser pulses and reconstructed 2D diffraction classes and 3D images.
AI.result: 2D classes of diffraction patterns were reconstructed to 15 Å resolution and 3D images to ~20 Å, while the 3D merged reciprocal-space intensity extended beyond 20 Å. The resolution discrepancy is likely due to heterogeneity from gas-phase compaction of the complexes.
AI.conclusion: With increased throughput, this approach could reveal in-situ structural details during mass spectrometry studies of biomolecules; improved sample delivery may enable ultrafast snapshot imaging of biological single particles in their native state beyond radiation-damage limits.

title: Acceleration of Newton's method for nonlinear algebraic systems by preflattening and elimination techniques
summary: In this paper, we propose a new approach called {\em preflattening} to speed up the resolution of nonlinear algebraic systems by Newton-type methods. Preflattening is meant to be for nonlinear systems what preconditioning is for linear ones. The idea is to transform the system into an equivalent one that is more favorable to Newton's method. To this end, we introduce the notion of {\em flatness}, which is intended to play for nonlinear systems a role similar to that of the condition number for linear systems. For a physical model of interest in the geosciences, namely the chemical equilibrium problem, we combine this strategy with the nonlinear elimination technique and demonstrate the value of the resulting approach through numerical simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "preflattening," a technique analogous to preconditioning but for nonlinear systems, to accelerate Newton-type methods by transforming systems into more favorable equivalent forms. It defines "flatness" (analogous to condition number) and applies the approach with nonlinear elimination to a geoscience chemical equilibrium problem, validating it via simulations.
AI.motivation: Newton-type methods for nonlinear algebraic systems can be slow or unstable. Preconditioning exists for linear systems but no analogous concept existed for nonlinear ones, motivating a transformation strategy to make systems more favorable to Newton's method.
AI.method: The authors propose "preflattening": transforming a nonlinear system into an equivalent one more amenable to Newton's method. They introduce the notion of "flatness," analogous to the condition number for linear systems. For the chemical equilibrium problem, they combine preflattening with nonlinear elimination.
AI.result: Numerical simulations on a geoscience chemical equilibrium model demonstrate the value of the combined preflattening and nonlinear elimination approach.
AI.conclusion: Preflattening serves as a nonlinear counterpart to preconditioning, and combining it with nonlinear elimination yields an effective approach for solving nonlinear algebraic systems, as shown on the chemical equilibrium problem.

title: A neural characteristic mapping method: Lagrangian PINNs based on flow maps for transport-dominated problems
summary: We propose a novel numerical method for transport-dominated problems using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs). In such problems, the solution can develop large gradients and fine structures over time. This is particularly challenging for classical PINNs, which represent the solution itself. In our approach, rather than the solution, we choose to approximate the flow map of the equation. The solution is then recovered by pulling back the exact initial condition, so that its fine structures are produced by the map rather than represented by the network. Our method is constructed by approximating the flow map of the equation with multiple PINNs, one per time subinterval, and composing them using the semigroup property of the flow, so that each network only has to represent a map close to the identity. To highlight the advantages of our method compared to classical PINNs or classical numerical schemes, we present numerical results on the linear advection equation, the incompressible Euler equation in vorticity formulation, the Vlasov-Poisson equation, and finally a drift-kinetic equation.

AI.tldr: A new PINN variant approximates the flow map (not the solution) of transport-dominated PDEs, composed over time subintervals via the semigroup property, enabling accurate capture of fine structures.
AI.motivation: Classical PINNs represent the solution itself, which struggles when solutions develop large gradients and fine structures over time in transport-dominated problems.
AI.method: Instead of the solution, approximate the equation's flow map with multiple PINNs, one per time subinterval, composed using the semigroup property of the flow; the solution is recovered by pulling back the exact initial condition, so fine structures come from the map rather than the network, and each network only represents a map close to identity.
AI.result: Numerical results demonstrate advantages over classical PINNs and classical numerical schemes on the linear advection equation, incompressible Euler equations (vorticity formulation), Vlasov-Poisson equation, and a drift-kinetic equation.
AI.conclusion: Approximating the flow map with composed subinterval PINNs is an effective approach for transport-dominated problems, handling fine structures and large gradients better than classical PINNs or numerical schemes.

title: Sharp stability near sums of ground states for fractional Schrödinger equations
summary: We study quantitative stability for the fractional Schrödinger equation $(-Δ)^s u+u-|u|^αu=0$ near finite sums of widely separated positive ground states. For every $n\ge1$, $0<s<1$, and Sobolev-subcritical exponent $α>0$, we estimate the $H^s$ distance to the family of such sums in terms of the $H^{-s}$ norm of the equation's residual. The optimal rate changes at $α=n/[2(n+2s)]$, with a logarithmic correction at the threshold. Above the threshold the rate is $t^{(n+2s)/(n+2s+1)}$; below it the exponent is $[(1+α)(n+2s)-n/2]/(n+2s+1)$. The proof combines uniform invertibility away from the translation modes with precise interaction estimates and a weighted correction of the approximate configuration. This correction resolves the translation interactions even when the nonlinearity has a small exponent. We also construct nonnegative configurations that attain these rates. The estimates quantify the effect of the algebraic decay of fractional ground states on stability.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes sharp quantitative stability estimates for the fractional Schrödinger equation near sums of widely separated positive ground states, with an optimal rate that changes at a threshold exponent α=n/[2(n+2s)].
AI.motivation: Understanding how stable the family of multi-soliton configurations is under perturbations of the fractional Schrödinger equation, and quantifying how the algebraic decay of fractional ground states affects this stability, particularly across a critical exponent threshold.
AI.method: The authors estimate the H^s distance to the family of sums via the H^{-s} norm of the equation's residual. The proof combines uniform invertibility away from translation modes, precise interaction estimates, and a weighted correction of the approximate configuration that resolves translation interactions even for small nonlinearity exponents.
AI.result: For every n≥1, 0<s<1, and Sobolev-subcritical α>0, the optimal rate changes at α=n/[2(n+2s)] (with a logarithmic correction at the threshold). Above the threshold the rate is t^{(n+2s)/(n+2s+1)}; below it the exponent is [(1+α)(n+2s)-n/2]/(n+2s+1). Nonnegative configurations attaining these rates are also constructed.
AI.conclusion: The estimates quantify the effect of algebraic decay of fractional ground states on stability and provide sharp, threshold-dependent stability rates for multi-soliton configurations of the fractional Schrödinger equation.

title: Prior or Feedback? What an LLM Uses When Adapting Neural Operators
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Science: Verification in the Age of AI Scientists. Equal contribution
summary: Do LLM scientific agents rely only on their initial task context, or do they adapt their decisions in response to experimental feedback? We study this question in neural operator adaptation, where a large language model (LLM) selects fine-tuning configurations under a limited trial budget. Across transfers within and between partial differential equation (PDE) families, the LLM achieves lower held-out test nRMSE than random search and Bayesian optimisation in nearly every matched comparison. Endpoint performance alone cannot distinguish what happens, so we verify each attribution with controlled interventions. Before observing any validation score, the LLM's first configuration already ranks near the top of the corresponding random-search pool, indicating a useful initial bias. A complementary cold-start intervention shows that the selected base learning rate shifts with the PDE description. Once feedback becomes available, reassigning validation scores among evaluated configurations changes the next proposal in every case tested, whereas a value-preserving rewrite produces no comparable aggregate effect. These interventions establish that the LLM's decision-level actions respond to the given task and observed outcomes, showing that it combines a task-dependent prior with sensitivity to experimental feedback.

AI.tldr: LLM agents for neural operator adaptation combine a task-dependent prior with sensitivity to experimental feedback, outperforming random search and Bayesian optimisation.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLM scientific agents rely only on their initial task context or adapt decisions based on experimental feedback.
AI.method: Study neural operator adaptation where an LLM selects fine-tuning configurations under a limited trial budget, with controlled interventions (cold-start, score reassignment, value-preserving rewrite).
AI.result: LLM achieves lower held-out test nRMSE than random search and Bayesian optimisation in nearly every matched comparison; first config ranks near top pre-feedback; base learning rate shifts with PDE description; reassigning validation scores changes next proposal.
AI.conclusion: The LLM's decision-level actions respond to the task and observed outcomes, combining a task-dependent prior with sensitivity to experimental feedback.

title: Data-Driven Free-Energy Learning from Trajectories via Structure-Preserving Exponential Time Differencing
summary: Structure-preserving numerical methods for gradient flows have been extensively developed when the governing equations and free energies are known. However, accurately predicting dynamics from observational data while preserving intrinsic physical properties remains challenging. Although neural operators, such as Fourier neural operators (FNOs), provide powerful data-driven approximations, their predictions do not inherently guarantee physical structure preservation. To address this challenge, we integrate deep learning with structure-preserving exponential time differencing (ETD) methods. Instead of directly learning the evolution operator, we introduce a *trajectory-inferred free energy* (TIFE), which reconstructs the unknown energy density from observed trajectories through a Duhamel-based learning framework. The learned energy determines the variational force and stabilization parameter, enabling structure-preserving numerical evolution. We further extend the framework to jointly identify the free energy and diffusion coefficient. Under suitable assumptions, we establish the maximum-bound principle, unconditional dissipation of the original learned energy, and error estimates incorporating discretization and inference errors. Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate energy recovery and reliable long-time predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper integrates deep learning with structure-preserving exponential time differencing (ETD) methods, introducing a trajectory-inferred free energy (TIFE) that reconstructs unknown energy density from observed trajectories via a Duhamel-based learning framework to guarantee physical structure preservation.
AI.motivation: Structure-preserving numerical methods require known governing equations and free energies, while data-driven neural operators (e.g., FNOs) do not inherently guarantee physical structure preservation. Accurately predicting dynamics from observational data while preserving intrinsic physical properties remains challenging.
AI.method: The framework integrates deep learning with structure-preserving ETD methods. Instead of directly learning the evolution operator, it introduces a trajectory-inferred free energy (TIFE) that reconstructs the unknown energy density from observed trajectories through a Duhamel-based learning framework. The learned energy determines the variational force and stabilization parameter, enabling structure-preserving evolution. The framework is further extended to jointly identify free energy and diffusion coefficient.
AI.result: Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate energy recovery and reliable long-time predictions.
AI.conclusion: Under suitable assumptions, the authors establish the maximum-bound principle, unconditional dissipation of the original learned energy, and error estimates incorporating discretization and inference errors.

title: Homogeneous solutions of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in arbitrary dimension
summary: For every integer $n\ge4$, we prove the existence of a $(-1)$-homogeneous solution of the stationary incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$ with an arbitrary locally Lipschitz $(-3)$-homogeneous force. The pressure is $(-2)$-homogeneous, and the solution is regular away from the origin. This extends the homogeneous existence theorem of Bang, Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie beyond dimension sixteen. The principal estimate combines a subcritical localized pressure identity with an elementary dyadic estimate for an auxiliary tangential vector field in a suitable finite Lebesgue space. Testing the Bernoulli equation at the homogeneous cancellation exponent then controls its positive part in $L^{\frac{(n-2)(n-1)}{2(n-3)}}(S^{n-1})$. The resulting estimate closes with the energy inequality in every fixed dimension. We also establish uniqueness throughout the classical homogeneous class for sufficiently small force. Using the same ideas, we also give a simplified proof of the known existence theorem for bounded compactly supported forces on $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n\ge5$. A general finite-exponent estimate for a scalar equation with divergence-free drift, together with a Euclidean version of the dyadic kernel estimate, bounds the positive Bernoulli function without BMO estimates or an iteration to obtain its supremum norm.

AI.tldr: The paper proves existence of (-1)-homogeneous solutions to stationary incompressible Navier-Stokes on R^n\{0} for all n≥4 with (-3)-homogeneous Lipschitz force, extending prior results beyond dimension 16, plus uniqueness for small force.
AI.motivation: The prior homogeneous existence theorem of Bang, Gui, Liu, Wang, and Xie was limited to dimensions up to sixteen. This work aims to establish existence in arbitrary dimensions n≥4.
AI.method: A subcritical localized pressure identity combined with an elementary dyadic estimate for an auxiliary tangential vector field in a finite Lebesgue space. Testing the Bernoulli equation at the homogeneous cancellation exponent controls its positive part in L^((n-2)(n-1)/(2(n-3)))(S^{n-1}), closing with the energy inequality in every fixed dimension.
AI.result: Existence of a regular-away-from-origin (-1)-homogeneous solution with (-2)-homogeneous pressure for any n≥4; uniqueness in the classical homogeneous class for sufficiently small force; a simplified proof of the known existence theorem for bounded compactly supported forces on R^n, n≥5.
AI.conclusion: A general finite-exponent estimate for a scalar equation with divergence-free drift, plus a Euclidean dyadic kernel estimate, bounds the positive Bernoulli function without BMO estimates or iteration to obtain its supremum norm.

title: Mathematical foundation of symmetric fast Fourier transform
summary: In this work, we study the fast Fourier transform (FFT) of discrete data with crystallographic symmetry, for which standard FFT algorithms incur substantial redundant computation. We establish a rigorous mathematical theory of the symmetric fast Fourier transform (SFFT) for $n$-dimensional crystallographic groups and propose the SFFT and symmetric inverse fast Fourier transform (SIFFT) algorithms. We derive symmetry-reduction formulas for both linear and translational symmetries and unify them into a recursive framework. We analyze the arithmetic complexity to obtain theoretical speedup factors relative to the standard FFT, and we confirm the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed methods by numerical experiments on representative three-dimensional space groups.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a rigorous theory and algorithms (SFFT/SIFFT) for computing the FFT of discrete data with crystallographic symmetry, eliminating redundant computation and achieving theoretical and empirical speedups over standard FFT.
AI.motivation: Standard FFT algorithms incur substantial redundant computation when applied to discrete data exhibiting crystallographic symmetry, since they ignore the underlying group structure.
AI.method: Establish a mathematical theory of the symmetric FFT for n-dimensional crystallographic groups; propose SFFT and SIFFT algorithms; derive symmetry-reduction formulas for linear and translational symmetries; unify them in a recursive framework; and analyze arithmetic complexity to obtain theoretical speedup factors.
AI.result: Theoretical speedup factors relative to standard FFT are derived, and numerical experiments on representative three-dimensional space groups confirm the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed methods.
AI.conclusion: The SFFT and SIFFT provide an effective, mathematically grounded approach to exploit crystallographic symmetry in FFT computation, reducing redundancy and improving efficiency.

title: Rigidity of a $Q$-curvature-type problem on $\mathbb{S}^N$ in every dimension $N\geq3$
summary: We prove that for every $N\geq 3$, every solution to the $Q$-curvature-type problem $$ αP_N u + (N-1)!\left(1-\frac{e^{Nu}}{\int_{\mathbb{S}^N} e^{Nu}dw}\right)=0 \ \ \ \ \ \mbox{on} \ \mathbb{S}^N $$ is constant, provided that $ α\ge\frac{1}{2}$ and $α\not =1$. The proof consists of a spectral gap estimate and pointwise estimates of the normalized density $\left(\int_{\mathbb{S}^N} e^{Nu}dw\right)^{-1}e^{Nu}$.

AI.tldr: For every $N\geq 3$, any solution to the $Q$-curvature-type equation on $\mathbb{S}^N$ is constant when $\alpha \geq 1/2$ and $\alpha \neq 1$.
AI.motivation: The $Q$-curvature-type problem on the sphere generalizes classical prescribing curvature equations; the case $\alpha = 1$ corresponds to the known Kazdan-Warner-type setting. Understanding rigidity/nonexistence of nonconstant solutions for other $\alpha$ is of interest.
AI.method: The proof combines a spectral gap estimate with pointwise estimates of the normalized density $\left(\int_{\mathbb{S}^N} e^{Nu}dw\right)^{-1}e^{Nu}$.
AI.result: Every solution is constant provided $\alpha \ge 1/2$ and $\alpha \neq 1$.
AI.conclusion: The equation admits only constant solutions in the range $\alpha \ge 1/2$, $\alpha \neq 1$, confirming a rigidity phenomenon.

title: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems
summary: Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems, from structural buckling to fluid and climate dynamics, yet they remain largely unexplored in deep learning. At a symmetry-breaking bifurcation, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption underlying most learned physical surrogates. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass. We evaluate Bi-FORK on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. Bi-FORK recovers the multimodal solution structure while scaling several orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches, opening generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems.

AI.tldr: Bi-FORK is a generative framework that learns one-to-many solution maps at symmetry-breaking bifurcations in high-dimensional physical systems.
AI.motivation: Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems but largely unexplored in deep learning. At symmetry-breaking bifurcations, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption of most learned physical surrogates.
AI.method: Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories via latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass.
AI.result: Evaluated on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. It recovers multimodal solution structure while scaling orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches.
AI.conclusion: Bi-FORK opens generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems.

title: Model Order Reduction for Parametric Dissipative Quantum Systems
summary: We consider reduced basis approximations of non-equilibrium steady states of parameter-dependent Lindbladians, whose ambient matrix space grows exponentially with system size. We give a unified structural view of the problem through its characterizations as an eigenvalue problem or as a trace-constrained source problem. Building on these characterizations, we propose a residual-driven reduced basis framework for both formulations. Under the assumption of a unique steady state, we derive residual-based state-error estimates, and establish (sub-)exponential convergence of the greedy algorithms under real-analytic parameter dependence of the problem data. Numerical experiments on boundary-driven Fermi--Hubbard and dissipative XYZ chains support the analysis and suggest that the trace-constrained greedy method offers the best overall balance of accuracy and computational cost.

AI.tldr: The paper develops residual-driven reduced basis approximations for non-equilibrium steady states of parameter-dependent Lindbladians, using eigenvalue and trace-constrained source formulations, with error estimates and greedy convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Non-equilibrium steady states of parameter-dependent Lindbladians live in matrix spaces that grow exponentially with system size, making direct computation prohibitively expensive. There is a need for efficient model reduction to handle this curse of dimensionality.
AI.method: The authors provide a unified structural view via two characterizations: an eigenvalue problem and a trace-constrained source problem. Based on these, they propose a residual-driven reduced basis framework for both formulations, deriving residual-based state-error estimates and analyzing greedy algorithm convergence under real-analytic parameter dependence.
AI.result: Under a unique steady-state assumption, they prove residual-based state-error estimates and establish (sub-)exponential convergence of greedy algorithms. Numerical experiments on boundary-driven Fermi-Hubbard and dissipative XYZ chains confirm the analysis and show the trace-constrained greedy method achieves the best accuracy/cost trade-off.
AI.conclusion: The proposed reduced basis framework offers an effective, theoretically grounded approach for approximating parameter-dependent Lindblad steady states, with the trace-constrained greedy variant being the most practical choice.

title: Uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions to the two-dimensional viscous Primitive Equations
summary: Global existence of Leray-Hopf (type) weak solutions to the viscous primitive equations in two or three dimensions was established by Lions--Temam--Wang \cite{Lions1,Lions2,Lions3,Lions4} in the 1990s; however, the corresponding uniqueness, no matter in two or three dimensions, has been a long standing open problem since then. In this paper, we solve this open problem in the two-dimensional case. Precisely, we prove the uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions, with arbitrary $L^2$ initial data, to the viscous primitive equations in a periodic channel, subject to impermeability and stress-free boundary conditions on the solid boundaries.

AI.tldr: The paper proves uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions to the 2D viscous primitive equations in a periodic channel with impermeability and stress-free boundary conditions for arbitrary L^2 initial data, resolving a long-standing open problem.
AI.motivation: Global existence of Leray-Hopf weak solutions to the viscous primitive equations was established in the 1990s, but uniqueness has remained open for decades in both 2D and 3D.
AI.method: Analytical proof of uniqueness for Leray-Hopf weak solutions in the two-dimensional setting within a periodic channel, subject to impermeability and stress-free boundary conditions.
AI.result: Uniqueness is established for arbitrary L^2 initial data in the 2D case.
AI.conclusion: The long-standing open problem of uniqueness of Leray-Hopf weak solutions is solved in the two-dimensional case.

title: A posteriori error estimation for coarse or distorted meshes
summary: Finite element simulations carried out on meshes issued from real-world geometries - patient-specific anatomies, scanned industrial parts, fractured media - almost never satisfy the shape-regularity assumptions under which classical a posteriori error analysis is written. Practitioners are therefore left without a quantitative answer to a very legitimate question: how wrong is my simulation when my mesh is coarse and contains badly shaped elements? In this work, we study to which extent equilibrated flux estimators can provide such an answer. Indeed, they deliver a guaranteed and fully computable upper bound of the energy-norm discretization error, with a constant equal to one; and, crucially for the present study, its derivation uses no shape-regularity, quasi-uniformity or angle condition. The only geometric ingredient is the Poincaré constant on a single cell, which Payne and Weinberger showed to be at most hK /pi on any convex cell K, however distorted (hK being the cell size). Mesh quality affects the local efficiency - the sharpness of the estimator - but never its reliability, so that the failure mode under distortion is pessimism rather than false confidence.

AI.tldr: Equilibrated flux estimators provide guaranteed, fully computable upper bounds on energy-norm discretization error with constant one, without requiring any shape-regularity assumptions; mesh distortion only degrades local sharpness (pessimism), never reliability.
AI.motivation: Finite element simulations on real-world geometries (patient-specific anatomies, scanned parts, fractured media) almost never satisfy the shape-regularity assumptions underlying classical a posteriori error analysis. Practitioners thus lack a quantitative answer to: how wrong is the simulation when the mesh is coarse or badly shaped?
AI.method: The study examines equilibrated flux estimators, which exploit their derivation requiring no shape-regularity, quasi-uniformity, or angle condition. The only geometric ingredient is the Poincaré constant on a single cell, bounded by hK/π for any convex cell K (Payne–Weinberger).
AI.result: Equilibrated flux estimators deliver a guaranteed, fully computable energy-norm error upper bound with constant equal to one, remaining valid on arbitrary distorted meshes. Mesh quality affects only local efficiency (sharpness).
AI.conclusion: Equilibrated flux estimators remain reliable under mesh distortion; the failure mode is pessimism (reduced sharpness) rather than false confidence. They offer a trustworthy a posteriori error quantification for real-world, badly shaped meshes.

title: Giaquinta's example revisited: the Liouville property for a class of nonuniformly elliptic equations in low dimensions

title: Variational Derivation of the Weak Form for Viscous Flows Involving Free Surfaces with Implications for Geodynamic Simulations
summary: Geodynamic simulations involve solving the Stokes equations, where boundary conditions play a crucial role in governing internal dynamics and surface topography evolution. A common approach is to model the interface in contact with air as a free surface. This interface is stress-free and deforms in response to internal force balances, which is essential for understanding processes ranging from rifted margins to subduction. However, a free surface can introduce instabilities and oscillations in the numerical solution, commonly known as the "drunken sailor" instability, forcing the use of small time steps. Geodynamic models therefore often employ stabilization terms based on the gravitational effect of free-surface motion. To date, these terms have been derived primarily on a heuristic basis. Here, we apply variational calculus to the energy-minimization formulation of incompressible Stokes flow. Using the Gateaux derivative, we derive the complete weak form for a deforming free-surface domain and show that the stabilization terms arise naturally from the free-surface assumption. We consider the linear-viscosity case and identify two boundary-integral contributions: one associated with internal viscous deformation and the other with gravitational body force. Two benchmark cases demonstrate the consistency of the derived formulation with previously proposed stabilization approaches. Our results provide a mathematical foundation for the commonly used gravity stabilization and identify an additional viscous boundary contribution.

AI.tldr: Applying variational calculus to energy-minimization of incompressible Stokes flow, the authors derive the complete weak form for a deforming free-surface domain, showing gravity stabilization terms arise naturally and identifying an extra viscous boundary term.
AI.motivation: Free-surface modeling in geodynamic Stokes simulations suffers from the "drunken sailor" instability, requiring small time steps. Existing gravity-based stabilization terms were derived heuristically rather than from first principles, lacking a rigorous mathematical foundation.
AI.method: The authors apply variational calculus to the energy-minimization formulation of incompressible Stokes flow. Using the Gateaux derivative, they derive the complete weak form for a deforming free-surface domain, considering the linear-viscosity case.
AI.result: The stabilization terms emerge naturally from the free-surface assumption. Two boundary-integral contributions are identified: one from internal viscous deformation and one from gravitational body force. Two benchmark cases confirm consistency with previously proposed stabilization approaches.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a mathematical foundation for the widely used gravity stabilization method and reveals an additional viscous boundary contribution not previously recognized.

title: Oblique boundary value problems for n-1type augmented Hessian equations
comment: Oblique boundary value problems. n-1 type Augmented Hessian equations. Global second-derivative estimates. Gradient estimates. Classical solvability
summary: In this paper, we study the global regularity of oblique boundary value problems for n-1 type augmented Hessian equations on a bounded domain, without imposing any convexity condition either on the domain or on the matrix-valued function in the n-1 type augmented Hessian equations. We establish a global existence and uniqueness theory for classical elliptic solutions by deriving global a priori estimates up to second-order derivatives. Besides the known applications for n-1 type Monge-Ampere operators in optimal transportation and geometric optics, the general theory here embraces equations raised by Li-Sheng, Some Dirichlet problems arising from conformal geometry. Pac. J. Math. 251, 2011, 337-359 and Guan-Qiu-Yuan, Fully nonlinear elliptic equations for conformal deformations of Chern-Ricci forms. Adv. Math. 343, 2019, 538-566.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes global existence and uniqueness of classical elliptic solutions for oblique boundary value problems of n-1 type augmented Hessian equations without convexity assumptions on the domain or matrix-valued function.
AI.motivation: Prior work on n-1 type augmented Hessian equations typically requires convexity conditions on the domain or the matrix-valued function. This paper aims to remove these restrictions and provide a general theory that covers existing applications in optimal transportation, geometric optics, and conformal geometry.
AI.method: Derive global a priori estimates up to second-order derivatives for oblique boundary value problems of n-1 type augmented Hessian equations, without convexity conditions, and use them to establish existence and uniqueness of classical elliptic solutions. Also connect the theory to Li-Sheng and Guan-Qiu-Yuan equations.
AI.result: A global existence and uniqueness theory for classical elliptic solutions is established via global a priori estimates up to second-order derivatives, with no convexity condition imposed on the domain or matrix-valued function.
AI.conclusion: The general theory unifies and extends known applications for n-1 type Monge-Ampere operators and embraces equations from conformal geometry by Li-Sheng and Guan-Qiu-Yuan.

title: A Fast and Stable Square-Root-Free Unitary Core-Chasing Algorithm
summary: Symmetric and unitary matrices are among the most important classes of structured matrices admitting efficient and stable eigenvalue algorithms. Notable examples include structure-preserving variants of the QR algorithm and their square-root-free counterparts. For unitary matrices, these algorithms were historically derived from recurrence relations for orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle. A matrix-based derivation using core chasing was later given in [3]; this family of algorithms is backward stable, but the underlying symmetries needed to cast out the square roots were not identified, and the question of structured backward stability was left open. In this paper we present a matrix-based derivation of the symmetric unitary core-chasing algorithm and use it to obtain a square-root-free variant. We give a matrix-based proof of backward stability and show that strict structured backward stability is impossible in general. Open-source Fortran code and numerical experiments demonstrate that the combination of exploiting the symmetry and removing the square roots reduces computation time without degrading accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper derives a matrix-based symmetric unitary core-chasing algorithm, obtains a square-root-free variant, proves backward stability, and shows strict structured backward stability is generally impossible.
AI.motivation: Symmetric and unitary matrices admit efficient stable eigenvalue algorithms, and core-chasing variants are backward stable, but the symmetries needed to remove square roots were unidentified and structured backward stability remained an open question.
AI.method: The authors give a matrix-based derivation of the symmetric unitary core-chasing algorithm, use it to construct a square-root-free variant, and provide a matrix-based proof of backward stability.
AI.result: They prove backward stability, show strict structured backward stability is impossible in general, and demonstrate via open-source Fortran code and numerical experiments that exploiting symmetry and removing square roots reduces computation time without degrading accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting unitary symmetry and eliminating square roots yields a faster core-chasing algorithm with preserved accuracy, though strict structured backward stability cannot be guaranteed in general.

title: Volume Sampling and Spectral Equalization in Randomized Alternating Projections
summary: We study a family of randomized alternating projection methods that alternate among subspaces spanned by subsets of \(n\) vectors from a prescribed set. We derive an explicit characterization of performance bounds when these subspaces are sampled with probabilities proportional to the volumes subtended by the vectors in their corresponding subsets. For each \(n\), the bound is obtained through an explicit nonlinear transformation of the spectrum of an associated matrix. Our analysis reveals an explicit spectral equalization mechanism that drives the spectrum toward improved conditioning as $n$ increases, establishing an unexpected connection between volume sampling and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. Furthermore, we introduce a computationally efficient uniform sampling scheme that achieves comparable theoretical guarantees through a specific relaxation strategy. Empirical results show that this relaxation method achieves convergence rates comparable to, and often better than, volume sampling, while avoiding the infeasibility of volume sampling at large scale. Besides the randomized Kaczmarz, these results also directly apply to randomized Gauss-Seidel and coordinate descent methods.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes randomized alternating projection methods over subspaces, deriving explicit performance bounds under volume-proportional sampling and introducing a practical uniform sampling relaxation.
AI.motivation: Randomized alternating projection methods are widely used, but their theoretical behavior under different sampling strategies—especially volume sampling—is not well characterized. Volume sampling offers strong guarantees but is computationally infeasible at scale, motivating the need for a deeper theoretical understanding and a tractable alternative.
AI.method: The authors study randomized alternating projections across subspaces spanned by subsets of n vectors. They derive explicit performance bounds when subspaces are sampled with probabilities proportional to subtended volumes, obtained via a nonlinear transformation of an associated matrix's spectrum. They also propose a uniform sampling scheme based on a specific relaxation strategy.
AI.result: An explicit spectral equalization mechanism emerges, improving conditioning as n grows, revealing an unexpected link between volume sampling and the Cayley-Hamilton theorem. Empirically, the relaxed uniform sampling scheme matches or surpasses volume sampling's convergence rates while remaining scalable.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a rigorous characterization of volume sampling for randomized alternating projections and a practical, efficient substitute. Results extend to randomized Kaczmarz, Gauss-Seidel, and coordinate descent methods.

title: Convexity preservation for first-order nonlinear evolution equations with Neumann-type boundary conditions
summary: We study preservation of spatial convexity for viscosity solutions of first order Hamilton-Jacobi evolution equations with Neumann-type boundary conditions in bounded convex domains. Under a monotonicity assumption on the Hamiltonian in the outward normal direction, every viscosity supersolution of the Neumann problem is also a state-constraint supersolution. This reduces the boundary difficulty to a state-constraint problem and enables us to prove convexity preservation via the convex-envelope argument established by Alvarez, Lasry and Lions (1997). We also obtain propagation estimates for semiconvexity and strong convexity under similar structural assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that spatial convexity is preserved for viscosity solutions of first-order Hamilton-Jacobi evolution equations with Neumann-type boundary conditions in bounded convex domains, under a monotonicity assumption on the Hamiltonian in the outward normal direction.
AI.motivation: Handling convexity preservation for Neumann boundary problems is difficult due to boundary complications. The authors aim to overcome these boundary difficulties.
AI.method: They show that, under a monotonicity assumption on the Hamiltonian in the outward normal direction, every viscosity supersolution of the Neumann problem is also a state-constraint supersolution. This reduces the boundary problem to a state-constraint problem, allowing use of the convex-envelope argument of Alvarez, Lasry and Lions (1997).
AI.result: Convexity preservation is established via the convex-envelope argument, and propagation estimates for semiconvexity and strong convexity are obtained under similar structural assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The monotonicity assumption on the Hamiltonian reduces the Neumann problem to a state-constraint problem, enabling convexity preservation and propagation estimates for semiconvexity and strong convexity.

title: Existence of pulse solutions in a bulk--surface reaction--diffusion system for cell polarization
summary: In this paper, we prove the existence of stationary pulse solutions for a bulk-surface reaction-diffusion system modeling cell polarization in two-dimensional domains. Using a singular perturbation method, we construct pulse solutions whose centers lie near non-degenerate critical points of a geometry-dependent potential expressed in terms of the Neumann Green's function, as formally predicted in \cite{watanabe2026}. The main analytical difficulty arises from the half-Laplacian induced by the logarithmic singularity of the Green's function, resulting in algebraically rather than exponentially decaying inner solutions. Our analysis may also serve as a useful guide for applying singular perturbation methods to other bulk-surface type systems.

AI.tldr: This paper proves existence of stationary pulse solutions for a bulk-surface reaction-diffusion model of cell polarization in 2D, constructed via singular perturbation near non-degenerate critical points of a geometry-dependent potential.
AI.motivation: Cell polarization is modeled by bulk-surface reaction-diffusion systems, and formal predictions (watanabe2026) suggested pulse solutions localized near critical points of a Green's-function-based potential. A rigorous proof was lacking.
AI.method: Singular perturbation method, constructing pulse solutions whose centers lie near non-degenerate critical points of a geometry-dependent potential expressed via the Neumann Green's function. Key difficulty: half-Laplacian from the logarithmic Green's singularity yields algebraically (not exponentially) decaying inner solutions.
AI.result: Existence of stationary pulse solutions is established, confirming the formal prediction. The inner solutions exhibit algebraic rather than exponential decay due to the half-Laplacian.
AI.conclusion: The results rigorously confirm prior formal predictions and the approach may guide singular perturbation analyses of other bulk-surface systems.

title: The Quality of Lattice Sequences for Arbitrary Sample Size
summary: Extensible lattices are a common choice of nodes for approximating multidimensional integrals by a sample mean, typically using sample sizes of the form $n = b^m$ for a prime base $b$ and non-negative integer $m$. However, a computational time budget or early termination due to hardware failure may prevent us from choosing the preferred number of samples. In this paper, we establish an upper bound on the figure of merit $P_α$ for extensible lattice sequences \emph{with arbitrary $n$}, derived as a worst-case error in a Banach space setting. We show that although the upper bound on $P_α$ can decay no faster than $\mathcal O(n^{-1})$ for general $n$, restricting $n$ to the form $n =λb^p$, where $λ$ is a fixed integer, we can recover the optimal decay of nearly $\mathcal O(n^{-α})$ as $p \to \infty$. We also investigate a related figure of merit, $P_{α,2}$, arising as a worst-case error for Hilbert spaces of integrands. We obtain a theoretical upper bound on $P_{α,2}$ in terms of $P_α$ for equal sample weights and show numerically that optimal sample weights can improve the cubature error bound even further.

AI.tldr: This paper bounds the figure of merit P_α (and P_{α,2}) for extensible lattice sequences with arbitrary sample size n, showing optimal decay ~O(n^{-α}) is recovered when n=λb^p.
AI.motivation: Extensible lattices typically use sample sizes n=b^m, but time budgets or hardware failures force arbitrary n; the error behavior for such n is not well understood.
AI.method: Derives an upper bound on P_α as a worst-case error in a Banach space setting for extensible lattice sequences with arbitrary n; also relates P_{α,2} (Hilbert space worst-case error) to P_α for equal sample weights, and tests optimal sample weights numerically.
AI.result: For general n, the P_α bound decays no faster than O(n^{-1}); restricting to n=λb^p (λ fixed integer) recovers near-optimal decay ~O(n^{-α}) as p→∞. Optimal sample weights further improve the cubature error bound numerically.
AI.conclusion: Extensible lattices retain near-optimal convergence for sample sizes of the form n=λb^p, and optimal weights can enhance error bounds.

title: Uniqueness in inverse elastic scattering from traction-free polygonal obstacles with a single incoming wave
summary: In this article, we establish uniqueness in the inverse problem of time-harmonic elastic scattering from a bounded, traction-free obstacle in two dimensions. For a single incident plane wave, it is proved that a connected polygonal obstacle is uniquely determined by the measured far-field pattern. The analysis is based on a reflection principle for the Navier equation under traction-free boundary conditions and unique continuation of elastic fields.

AI.tldr: This paper proves uniqueness for the inverse time-harmonic elastic scattering problem from a bounded traction-free obstacle in 2D. Using a single incident plane wave, a connected polygonal obstacle is uniquely determined by its far-field pattern.
AI.motivation: Uniqueness in inverse elastic scattering from obstacles is a fundamental question. Establishing that a single measurement determines the obstacle is important but nontrivial, especially for the traction-free boundary condition.
AI.method: The proof uses a reflection principle for the Navier equation under traction-free boundary conditions, combined with unique continuation of elastic fields.
AI.result: It is shown that a connected polygonal obstacle is uniquely determined by the measured far-field pattern from a single incident plane wave.
AI.conclusion: Uniqueness holds for the inverse time-harmonic elastic scattering problem from bounded, traction-free polygonal obstacles in two dimensions.

title: Uniform Approximation for Operator Learning on Compact Sets
summary: We study uniform approximation for operator learning on compact subsets of Banach spaces. We bound the recovery dimensions and the number of network parameters in terms of compact-set complexity, the target gauge, and recovery stability. For bounded linear operators with a separable domain, we characterize gauge approximability by coordinate decompositions with a common vanishing gauge and arbitrarily small additive errors. Their partial sums give a fixed family of nonlinear encoder--decoder pairs. We prove that nonlinear recovery with a common vanishing gauge and a rank bound depending only on the model dimension is equivalent to the uniform approximation property (UAP). We also obtain linear recovery estimates with the same rank bound and an operator version for the linear factors of nonlinear targets. For Barron operators taking values in a Banach space $Y$ of type $p\in(1,2]$ and admitting a Bochner-integrable density, sampling gives the rate $N^{-(1-1/p)}$ for the expected $L^p(λ;Y)$ error, where $λ$ is a probability measure on the input compact set. For fixed finite-dimensional factors and a class of Hölder maps, we obtain matching upper and lower parameter bounds at fixed sufficiently large depth. Classical sampling and truncation examples provide explicit recovery maps, and a nonlinear integral operator illustrates the parameter bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper develops uniform approximation theory for operator learning on compact subsets of Banach spaces, bounding recovery dimensions and network parameters via compact-set complexity, target gauge, and recovery stability, and connects nonlinear recovery to the uniform approximation property (UAP).
AI.motivation: Operator learning lacks a general uniform approximation theory on compact Banach-space subsets. The work aims to bound recovery dimensions and network parameters in terms of intrinsic quantities and to characterize when nonlinear recovery is feasible.
AI.method: Uses gauge approximability via coordinate decompositions with common vanishing gauge; nonlinear encoder-decoder pairs from partial sums; rank bounds tied to model dimension; sampling for Barron operators (type p Bochner-integrable density); analysis of finite-dimensional factors and Hölder maps at fixed large depth.
AI.result: For bounded linear operators with separable domain, characterizes gauge approximability; shows nonlinear recovery with common vanishing gauge and dimension-dependent rank bound is equivalent to UAP; obtains linear recovery estimates and an operator version for linear factors; sampling gives rate N^{-(1-1/p)} for expected L^p error; matching upper/lower parameter bounds for fixed finite-dimensional factors and Hölder maps at large depth.
AI.conclusion: Provides a unified framework linking compact-set complexity, gauge, and stability to recovery/parameter bounds for operator learning, with sharp sampling rates and parameter bounds, illustrated by classical sampling/truncation and a nonlinear integral operator.

title: Boundary Control of Two-dimensional Point-Vortex Systems
summary: In this article, we investigate the boundary controllability of finite point-vortex systems in bounded multiply connected planar Lipschitz domains. The controls are applied locally on an arbitrary nonempty relatively open subset of the boundary. Zero incoming vorticity is assumed at the inflow part of the boundary. For time-dependent controls, we prove exact trajectory controllability along arbitrary prescribed collision-free vortex paths remaining away from the boundary. For stationary controls, we prove exact endpoint controllability associated with mutually disjoint real-analytic arcs. The proofs rely on harmonic interpolation, localized Runge approximation, and an implicit-function argument. The optimal control minimizing the length of trajectories is also studied. We prove the nonexistence of minimizers within classes of slightly smooth controls, and establish existence when the control time and the size of the control are penalized.

AI.tldr: This paper studies boundary controllability of finite point-vortex systems in bounded multiply connected planar Lipschitz domains, with controls applied locally on the boundary under zero incoming vorticity.
AI.motivation: To understand how localized boundary controls can steer point vortices in multiply connected domains, addressing exact trajectory and endpoint controllability along prescribed paths.
AI.method: Harmonic interpolation, localized Runge approximation, and an implicit-function argument; optimal control minimizing trajectory length is also analyzed.
AI.result: Exact trajectory controllability for time-dependent controls along arbitrary collision-free vortex paths away from the boundary; exact endpoint controllability for stationary controls via disjoint real-analytic arcs. No minimizers exist among slightly smooth controls, but existence holds when control time and control size are penalized.
AI.conclusion: Localized boundary controls achieve exact controllability of point vortices in multiply connected Lipschitz domains; optimal control existence requires penalizing both time and control size.

title: A structure-preserving neural density functional for the ions of a polymer electrolyte
summary: Predicting the structure and response of inhomogeneous polymer electrolytes requires a description of ion correlations that retains molecular-scale accuracy while remaining transferable across spatial scales and geometries. We develop a neural density functional for electrolytes that preserves spatial symmetries, thermodynamic integrability and the Noether identities, with perfect screening recovered in stable, noncritical bulk states. Its nonlinear density dependence captures the concentration-dependent correlations missed by a pair closure, including a crossover from enhanced to suppressed long-wavelength number fluctuations at strong coupling. The functional describes density profiles at an untrained salt concentration and predicts bulk structure factors and the long-wavelength number response. Trained solely on planar density and internal-force profiles from molecular dynamics, the functional predicts ionic structure in larger domains and in two-dimensional external fields. On the same ion data, it is more accurate than three other neural density-functional architectures and keeps its accuracy with a quarter of the training runs, where the errors of the best alternative grow by about two thirds. The spatial transferability provides a necessary foundation for connecting molecular correlations to continuum predictions at larger scales.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a physics-informed neural density functional for inhomogeneous polymer electrolytes that preserves spatial symmetries, thermodynamic integrability, and Noether identities, enabling accurate, transferable predictions of ionic structure across scales and geometries.
AI.motivation: Predicting the structure and response of inhomogeneous polymer electrolytes requires ion correlations described with molecular-scale accuracy that remain transferable across spatial scales and geometries—something pair closures fail to provide.
AI.method: They construct a neural density functional that enforces spatial symmetries, thermodynamic integrability, and Noether identities, with perfect screening recovered in stable noncritical bulk states, and a nonlinear density dependence trained solely on planar density and internal-force profiles from molecular dynamics.
AI.result: The functional captures concentration-dependent correlations beyond pair closures, including an enhanced-to-suppressed crossover of long-wavelength number fluctuations at strong coupling; it predicts profiles at untrained salt concentrations, bulk structure factors, ionic structure in larger domains and 2D external fields, outperforming three other neural density-functional architectures and retaining accuracy with a quarter of the training runs (where the best alternative's errors grow by ~two thirds).
AI.conclusion: The functional's spatial transferability provides a necessary foundation for connecting molecular correlations to continuum predictions at larger scales.

title: Long time dynamics for complex Ginzburg-Landau equations on three-dimensional Riemannian manifolds
summary: We study the energy-subcritical and energy-critical complex Ginzburg-Landau equations on three-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. We establish the asymptotic behavior of solutions via a purely energy-based approach and subsequently prove a fast/slow dichotomy of the solutions. Moreover, for the slow solution, we show that the solution converges to an explicit asymptotic profile. In particular, we obtain a precise description of both the amplitude and the phase of the leading-order dynamics. As a by-product, the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation approximation yields global weak solutions to the energy-subcritical and energy-critical defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equations on compact three-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. We also investigate the long time behavior of the solutions to the energy-subcritical and energy-critical complex Ginzburg-Landau equations on a class of complete noncompact three-dimensional Riemannian manifolds and prove decay of global solutions under suitable geometric assumptions.

AI.tldr: Study of complex Ginzburg-Landau equations (energy-subcritical and critical) on 3D Riemannian manifolds, establishing asymptotic behavior, a fast/slow dichotomy, explicit profile convergence, and NLS approximation.
AI.motivation: Energy-subcritical and critical complex Ginzburg-Landau equations on 3D Riemannian manifolds lack a precise asymptotic description of solutions, including amplitude and phase dynamics, and the link to defocusing nonlinear Schrödinger equations on such geometries.
AI.method: A purely energy-based approach to derive asymptotic behavior, proving a fast/slow dichotomy; for slow solutions, convergence to an explicit asymptotic profile with detailed amplitude and phase description. Also uses the CGL approximation to obtain solutions, with analysis on compact and noncompact manifolds.
AI.result: Established asymptotic behavior and fast/slow dichotomy; proved slow solutions converge to an explicit profile with precise leading-order amplitude and phase; derived global weak solutions to defocusing NLS on compact 3D manifolds; on noncompact manifolds, proved decay of global solutions under suitable geometric assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The energy-based framework characterizes CGL dynamics on 3D manifolds and yields NLS solutions as a by-product, with decay on noncompact manifolds under geometric conditions.

title: asdex: Automatic Sparse Differentiation in JAX
summary: Many tasks in scientific computing and machine learning require the Jacobian or Hessian matrix of a function. Automatic differentiation (AD) computes these derivatives to machine precision, but materializing a dense $m \times n$ Jacobian requires $n$ forward-mode or $m$ reverse-mode AD passes, one per column or row. For a large class of functions, each output depends on only a few inputs, making the derivative matrix sparse. Automatic sparse differentiation (ASD) exploits this structure in four steps: detection of the input-agnostic sparsity pattern, coloring of a graph to group columns or rows that can share an AD pass, compressed differentiation to compute a compressed derivative matrix with one AD pass per color, and finally decompression into the original sparsity pattern. The number of colors, and hence of AD passes, is often independent of the problem dimension: a banded Jacobian with $b$ contiguous bands, for instance, only ever requires $b$ colors, regardless of its size. asdex offers the first standalone ASD toolkit in the popular JAX ecosystem. With asdex.jacobian and asdex.hessian, it provides sparse drop-in replacements for jax.jacobian and jax.hessian.

AI.tldr: asdex is the first standalone automatic sparse differentiation (ASD) toolkit in JAX, offering sparse drop-in replacements (asdex.jacobian, asdex.hessian) for jax.jacobian and jax.hessian.
AI.motivation: Computing dense Jacobians/Hessians with AD requires n forward or m reverse passes, but for many functions each output depends on few inputs, making derivative matrices sparse. Exploiting this sparsity reduces the number of AD passes (often independent of problem dimension, e.g., b colors for a banded Jacobian).
AI.method: ASD via four steps: (1) input-agnostic sparsity pattern detection, (2) graph coloring to group columns/rows sharing an AD pass, (3) compressed differentiation with one AD pass per color, and (4) decompression into the original sparsity pattern.
AI.result: asdex provides the first standalone ASD toolkit in JAX, with asdex.jacobian and asdex.hessian as sparse drop-in replacements for jax.jacobian and jax.hessian.
AI.conclusion: ASD reduces AD passes by exploiting sparsity, and asdex brings this capability to the JAX ecosystem as drop-in replacements.

title: Some counterexamples concerning a model of eradication of invasive species
summary:
In this note we study the regularity properties of the \emph{Effort Function $E(β)$}. This can be defined as the minimal $L^1$-norm of the control $\tilde α(x) \geq 0$ so that the PDE $$U_t = ΔU + f(U) - \tilde α(t,x) U, \quad U \in [0,1], %\ \tilde α\geq 0,$$ admits a traveling profile $U(x - βt)$ connecting $0$ to $1$. The above PDE models the evolution of an invasive species, where the control $\tilde α(t,x)$ describes the percentage amount of species removal.
  In the literature some conditions are assumed on the properties of $f(U)$ and (consequently) on the effort function $E(β)$, the main ones being that the traveling profile has a simple structure and that the effort function can be used as an anisotropic perimeter to generated a cost function over sets of finite perimeter.
  This note gives some examples showing that in the interesting cases, i.e. when the PDE has a non trivial dynamics, these assumptions are in general not satisfied. We also show that $E(β)$ is in general only $C^1$.

AI.tldr: This note examines regularity of the Effort Function E(β), the minimal L¹-norm of removal control allowing a traveling wave. It shows common assumptions in the literature fail in nontrivial cases and that E(β) is generally only C¹.
AI.motivation: Existing literature assumes conditions on f(U) and E(β): that the traveling profile has a simple structure and that E(β) can serve as an anisotropic perimeter generating a cost function over finite-perimeter sets. The author seeks to test whether these assumptions hold in the genuinely interesting regime of the PDE (nontrivial dynamics).
AI.method: The paper constructs explicit examples (counterexamples) of the reaction-diffusion model U_t = ΔU + f(U) − ᾱ(t,x)U, U ∈ [0,1], with control ᾱ ≥ 0, analyzing the resulting Effort Function E(β) as the minimal L¹-norm yielding a traveling profile U(x − βt) connecting 0 to 1.
AI.result: The assumed structural properties of the traveling profile and the use of E(β) as an anisotropic perimeter are shown not to hold in general when the PDE has nontrivial dynamics. Moreover, E(β) is in general only C¹, not smoother.
AI.conclusion: The commonly adopted assumptions on E(β) are unjustified in the interesting cases; the effort function's regularity is limited to C¹, which constrains its use as an anisotropic perimeter in cost-function constructions.

title: Pointwise Structures and Background Perturbation Analyses for Thermal Non-equilibrium Irrotational Flows in Three Space Dimensions
summary: In this paper, both the pointwise space-time structures of the solution for a three-dimensional model describing gas dynamics in thermal non-equilibrium and the corresponding background stabilities within the $L^p$ framework are investigated under the small initial perturbation assumption and the irrotationality condition. Our main tools are the modified Green's function according to the irrotationality condition, a priori energy method and a refined decay estimates of products composed of the entropy function and high-order derivatives.

AI.tldr: The paper studies pointwise space-time structures and L^p background stability for a 3D gas dynamics model in thermal non-equilibrium under small perturbations and irrotationality.
AI.motivation: Understanding solution structures and stability of a 3D thermal non-equilibrium gas dynamics model within an L^p framework is important for characterizing its long-term behavior.
AI.method: Uses a modified Green's function adapted to the irrotationality condition, an a priori energy method, and refined decay estimates of products of the entropy function and high-order derivatives.
AI.result: Obtains pointwise space-time structures of the solution and establishes corresponding background stabilities under small initial perturbation and irrotationality assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The modified Green's function and refined decay techniques successfully characterize the solution and its L^p stability for the model.

title: Continuity and monotonicity of weighted perimeters of convex bodies
summary: We investigate weighted perimeters of convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Our main result states that the weighted perimeter is continuous with respect to the Hausdorff metric for every radial weight function. We also establish monotonicity under inclusion under suitable assumptions on the radial weight, and show that these assumptions are sharp. These results are applied to show the existence of minimizers for a shape optimization problem.

AI.tldr: The paper studies weighted perimeters of convex bodies in R^n, proving continuity w.r.t. the Hausdorff metric for arbitrary radial weights, establishing sharp monotonicity conditions under inclusion, and applying these to a shape optimization existence result.
AI.motivation: Weighted perimeters are central to geometric measure theory and anisotropic shape optimization, but their basic regularity (continuity, monotonicity) under general radial weights was not fully understood.
AI.method: Analytic study of weighted perimeter functionals for convex bodies in R^n, using the Hausdorff metric topology and conditions on radial weight functions; monotonicity examined under inclusion with sharpness examples.
AI.result: Weighted perimeter is continuous w.r.t. the Hausdorff metric for every radial weight; monotonicity under inclusion holds under suitable assumptions on the radial weight, and these assumptions are shown to be sharp.
AI.conclusion: These structural results are applied to prove existence of minimizers for a shape optimization problem.

title: Uniqueness for TV-regularized inverse problems with source in divergence form
summary: Inverse source problems in divergence form consist in finding a vector field with prescribed support S, whose divergence is the Laplacian of some observed potential. In this paper, we assume the unknown vector field is a vector-valued measure, and we study the corresponding least square inversion problems, regularized by penalizing the total variation, without discretizing the criterion nor the unknown. We prove that this problem has a unique minimizer in the case where S is a slender set; i.e., it has zero Lebesgue measure and each connected component of its complement has infinite Lebesgue measure. The proof relies on a refinement of Smirnov's decomposition of divergence-free measures [62] which is of independent interest.

AI.tldr: The paper studies least-square inversion for divergence-form inverse source problems where the unknown is a vector-valued measure supported on a prescribed set S, regularized by total variation. It proves uniqueness of the minimizer when S is a slender set, using a refined Smirnov decomposition of divergence-free measures.
AI.motivation: Inverse source problems in divergence form aim to recover a vector field with prescribed support S whose divergence equals the Laplacian of an observed potential. The authors seek a fully continuous (non-discretized) formulation and well-posedness guarantees for the corresponding variational inversion.
AI.method: The unknown vector field is modeled as a vector-valued measure, and the inversion is formulated as a least-square problem regularized by penalizing the total variation, without discretizing the criterion or the unknown. The analysis relies on a refined version of Smirnov's decomposition of divergence-free measures.
AI.result: The problem is shown to admit a unique minimizer when the support set S is slender, i.e., it has zero Lebesgue measure and each connected component of its complement has infinite Lebesgue measure.
AI.conclusion: Total-variation-regularized least-square inversion of divergence-form source problems is well-posed under the slender support assumption. The refined Smirnov decomposition used in the proof is of independent interest.

title: Weighted Gagliardo--Nirenberg Inequalities of Grushin Type: Symmetries, Compactness, and Optimizers
summary: In this paper, we study a family of weighted Gagliardo--Nirenberg interpolation inequalities associated with Grushin--type operators on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^m$. Specifically, we examine how to control the weighted norm $\||x|^βu \|_{L^B}$ by balancing fractional derivatives $D_x^s u$ with weighted derivatives $|x|^b D_y^r u$. Using two--parameter scaling, spatial translations, and Littlewood--Paley decompositions, we map out exact parameter conditions and demonstrate that the scaling exponents are both necessary and optimal. For multi-parameter weighted extensions, we leverage Khintchine-type random sums to show why $Q \ge 2$ is strictly required. When $x$ and $y$ are radially symmetric, two key advantages emerge: the allowable parameter range for the weights expands, and compact embeddings of the energy space into $L^p$, $2 < p < B$, are completely restored. We establish this compactness through two complementary tools, geometric covering arguments and a generalized three--norm version of Strauss's lemma, that yields explicit pointwise weighted decay estimates.
